item.title: Molecular Assembly Enumeration vs. 1D Dictionary Compression Across the Nano-DrugBank Small-Molecule Repository
item.description: Assembly Theory (AT) defines the Molecular Assembly Index (MA) as the minimal number of recursive bonddisjoint subgraph-joining steps required to construct a 2D molecular graph [1, 2, 4], whereas critics from Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) contend that empirical MA rankings collapse to standard 1D dictionary compression applied to molecular strings [5, 6, 15]. Here, we evaluate MA against wrapped zlib (RFC 1950), headerless raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951), and header-free 256-ASCII Welch LZW across the Chodera Lab Nano-DrugBank small-molecule repository (N = 5,653, curated from DrugBank 4.5.0) [20–24] using the C++ branchand-bound solver (assemblycpp-v5) [4] under operating-system process isolation on an Apple M3 Ultra workstation. Applying RDKit valence sanitization, parent-fragment desalting (60 salts), stereochemistry-stripped Kekulé MDL V2000 serialization, and a 600 s per-subprocess wall-clock timeout yielded 5,520 resolved records (97.65%; MA in [1, 36], median MA = 14, median subprocess wall time 15.42 ms, mean 3,051 ms; conditional on the inspected two-argument repository runner pending a hash-logged rerun), 35 RDKit valence rejections (0.62%), and 98 computationally unresolved valid graphs (1.73%): 87 with subprocess runtime right-censored at 600 s (median Nheavy = 77) and 11 macrocycles/polypeptides (median Nheavy = 128) explicitly logging the solver's internal Subgraph enumeration limit reached (ENUM_MAX = 50,000,000) diagnostic between 375.8 and 578.2 s. Among resolved records (median Nheavy = 23), 2,429 (44.00%) satisfy MA ≥ 15 [1, 2]. Per-character compression ratios span more than twofold ranges within fixed-MA slices, and in in-sample linear ordinary least-squares (OLS) models adjusting for heavy-atom count (Nheavy), compressed lengths explain 38.6% (DEFLATE: partial r = +0.6212) and 32.0% (Welch LZW: partial r = +0.5656) of Nheavy-adjusted MA variance on stereochemistrystripped canonical parent SMILES (38.4% and 31.7% across n = 5,274 unique parent strings; 42.9% and 38.8% on Kekulé charge/isotope-stripped V2000 graph SMILES, or 42.3% and 38.1% across n = 5,254 unique keys). Across all tested specifications, 57.1%–68.3% of in-sample Nheavy-adjusted linear MA variance remains unexplained, showing that the evaluated 1D SMILES compressors and 2D MA are positively correlated yet not linearly interchangeable.

item.title: Secondary Organic Aerosol Formation from Cleaning Product Use in a Residential Kitchen
item.description: Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) can form indoors when volatile organic compounds (VOCs), commonly emitted from the use of scented cleaning products and other chemical products, undergo oxidation and condense onto aerosols. Indoor oxidants can come from a variety of sources, including the use of chlorine bleach for surface cleaning and disinfection, operation of germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) lamps for air disinfection, and penetration of ozone (O3) from the outdoor environment. During the Consumer products, Lights, and Environmental Air cleaning in Normal conditions (CLEAN) Home Study, we measured SOA formation in a real home after performing surface cleaning with a scented all-purpose cleaning liquid and subsequently introducing different indoor oxidant scenarios. Six oxidant scenarios were tested, including (1) bleach surface cleaning, (2) O3 injection, (3) 222 nm GUV (GUV222) lamp operation, (4) 254 nm GUV (GUV254) lamp operation, and bleach surface cleaning with subsequent (5) GUV222 or (6) GUV254 lamp operation. Spraying the cleaning liquid emitted high concentrations of large primary particles and monoterpenes indoors. SOA formation occurred after cleaning liquid application and subsequent oxidant introduction for all oxidant scenarios except for bleach cleaning without subsequent GUV illumination. The oxidant scenario that led to the most SOA formation was bleach cleaning with GUV254 lamp operation. We used a chemical kinetic model to simulate monoterpene and aerosol concentrations indoors during cleaning liquid experiments with three oxidant scenarios: O3 injection, GUV222 lamp operation, and GUV254 lamp operation. We compared model results to our measurements for these select experiments. Results from this study demonstrate that indoor cleaning activities can lead to significant SOA formation in real indoor environments.

item.title: Transducing a CO2 Concentration Gradient into Electrical Energy through Copper–Ethylenediamine Coordination
item.description: A gas-phase concentration gradient contains Gibbs free energy, while converting this energy into electricity requires a chemical transduction mechanism. Here, we convert a CO2 concentration gradient into a Cu redox-potential difference through copper–ethylenediamine coordination. Ethylenediamine (eda) acts as a bifunctional molecular transducer: its coordination stabilizes the Cu2+ state, whereas CO2-induced protonation of eda diminishes coordination ability and stabilizes the metallic Cu. A cell consisting of copper electrodes and copper–ethylenediamine electrolyte generates an open-circuit voltage of 120 mV under a CO2/N2 gradient. A peak power density of 26.3 mW m−2 was achieved with a dialysis membrane, and Faradaic current was sustained for approximately 48 h. pH-dependent redox potentials and CO2 concentration-dependent pH shifts account for the generated open-circuit voltage. These results demonstrate a molecular strategy for coupling the chemical-potential difference associated with a CO2 concentration gradient to electrical output through linked acid–base, coordination, and redox equilibria without direct CO2 reduction.

item.title: Rh(III)-Catalyzed Regiodivergent Enantioselective C2- and C4–H Alkylation of Indoles
item.description: Switchable regiodivergent asymmetric synthesis constitutes a powerful paradigm in asymmetric catalysis, which greatly expands synthetic versatility and allows the efficient assembly of structurally diverse chiral molecules. Herein, we report a switchable regiodivergent enantioselective C–H functionalization of indoles with nitroalkenes, delivering a tunable platform to access C2- and C4-functionalized chiral indole derivatives with high efficiency, as well as excellent regio- and enantioselectivity (up to 97% yield, 96% ee, and >10:1 rr). Simply tuning the reaction parameters enables divergent C–H activation and enantioselective functionalization of electronically similar C(sp2)–H bonds within indole frameworks. Combined experimental and computational studies elucidate the mechanistic origins governing this remarkable regio- and enantioselectivity.

item.title: Selectivity for Fe versus Carbonyl Centered Silylation in Low-Valent β-Diketiminate Fe Complexes
item.description: Understanding the changes in reactivity and selectivity engendered by weak-field supporting ligands and multimetallic complexes offers new opportunities in organometallic chemistry. Here, we examine the selectivity of reactions of silyl electrophiles with monometallic iron-carbonyl complexes, which can lead to silylation either at the metal to form a silyl complex, or at a CO ligand to give a carbyne complex. The first mode of reactivity is common with classic organometallic complexes, and the latter has been observed more recently with complexes with strong-field ligands. More recently, bridging CO complexes with weak-field β-diketiminate ligands have been observed to give carbyne products as well, implying that the bridging CO ligands are nucleophilic in this environment. However, it was not clear whether the key determinant of CO reactivity was the ligand field strength or the bridging of the CO ligand. Here, these influences are decoupled by studying silylation of monomeric iron(0) dicarbonyl and tricarbonyl complexes with the same weak-field β-diketiminate ligand. We show that silylation at the iron, at the CO, or at THF can dominate. A particularly interesting product comes from THF silylation, followed by nucleophilic attack by Fe to give ring-opening and very rapid migration of a transient iron-alkyl complex to CO. DFT studies confirm that the β-diketiminate supported complexes undergo much more rapid alkyl migration than the analogous reaction in classic cyclopentadienyliron complexes. Overall, this work gives insights into ligand effects on reactivity for silylation and on alkyl insertion/CO migration.

item.title: Temporal programming of pH in enzyme-encapsulated artificial cells: role of differential membrane permeability
item.description: Coupling autocatalytic reaction networks and membrane-regulated transport of species within confined compartments provides a powerful strategy for engineering programmable dynamics in artificial cells. Here, we demonstrate temporal control of pH in phospholipid vesicles by encapsulating glucose oxidase (GOx) and urease enzymes, which respectively generate acidic and basic products from glucose and urea. We first explore the glucose-GOx reaction under confinement within the synthetic vesicles, combining experiments with simulations to find conditions for a pH clock reaction; a switch from base to acid after a time delay. We show that product entrapment results in a pH gradient between the internal and external solution and accelerates the reaction. By varying lipid composition, we find that the clock time increases with membrane thickness, consistent with glucose permeability regulating reaction kinetics under confinement. Building on these transport-limited dynamics, we couple the antagonistic GOx and urease reactions either in separate vesicle populations or within the same vesicle. Co-encapsulation produces an autonomous pH pulse in base, driven by differential membrane transport and product localisation. The pH clock and pulse amplitude and timescales can be tuned by initial concentrations, oxygen transfer rate from the air and volume fraction of the vesicles. Together, these findings establish how membrane-regulated feedback, substrate delay and product retention can be used to control the timescales of pH changes in artificial cells.

item.title: Evaluating Boltz-2 prediction of mutation-induced protein–ligand affinity changes
item.description: Protein mutations can affect how a protein binds a ligand and this may contribute to drug resistance as well as variability in patient responses to treatment. However, experimentally measuring binding affinities across numerous variants in real life is costly. Here we evaluated the accuracy of Boltz-2, a protein computational model used for biomolecular structure and binding-affinity prediction, by using experimentally determined reference-variant protein-ligand pairs collected from four independent data sources under the same experimental conditions. Boltz-2 predictions generally align with experimental trends, but the magnitude of large affinity changes, especially for mutations with indirect effects on ligand binding, is systematically underestimated. Structural analysis between predicted protein models by Boltz-2 and structures from lab data was compared side by side, further revealing that even accurate predictions between mutant protein-ligand structures from Boltz-2 could not guarantee accurate affinitychange predictions. These findings suggest that Boltz-2 is useful for variant prioritization and hypothesis generation but has limitations in quantitative mutation-effect prediction. They also highlight the value of matched reference-variant affinity data for benchmarking and improving future biomolecular models.

item.title: FOdorant conformational ensembles encode topology, molecular size and polar-surface coherence, not shape
item.description: Odor is widely modelled as three-dimensional shape recognition: a flexible odorant presents a 300 K conformer ensemble to a receptor repertoire, implying that perceptual breadth peaks at an intermediate number of accessible shapes and that explicit 3D representations outperform 2D molecular graphs. We test both predictions under a cryptographically pre-registered plan across catalogue profiles (n = 4,808), human psychophysics (n = 304) and heterologous receptor arrays (n = 294). Computing 300 K GFN2-xTB ensembles at a 200-conformer ceiling for all 1,821 flexible cohort members (106,526 conformers) and benchmarking 21 neural representations across 10 seeds, we find that neither claim holds. Conformational entropy saturates by 28 conformers (88% attained at a ceiling of 20), excluding an interior breadth optimum sixfold below the populated range (β2 = +0.0080, 95% CI -0.0014 to +0.0172). No 3D representation outperforms a capacity-matched or descriptor-augmented 2D graph. Out-of-sample-replicated confound analyses show that 3D shape dispersion vanishes once chain topology is controlled; instead, breadth reflects coarse topological flexibility (peaking at 9.2 rotatable bonds), molecular extent and polar-surface coherence (concave β2 = -0.0264). Keywords: conformational ensemble · odor breadth · molecular representation · Artificial Intelligence · Graph Neural Network

item.title: Metal Fluorides as Heterogeneous Base Catalysts: Exceptional C-C Bond Formation Activity from LaF3
item.description: Metal fluoride surfaces have potential as heterogeneous base catalysts. A systematic evaluation of rare-earth and alkaline-earth fluorides demonstrated the exceptional C-C bond formation activity of LaF3, rivaling or exceeding that of Mg-Al hydrotalcite. Hammett and kinetic isotope effect studies identified nitroalkane activation by basic sites as vital to this catalysis.

item.title: Models of Cofactors B12 and F430: Can Corrinoids Stabilize Nickel(I)?
item.description: We have examined four sterically constrained corrinoid ligands vis-à-vis their ability to stabilize low-oxidation-state transition metal centers, especially Ni(I), using modern DFT calculations with two exchange-correlation functionals (OLYP-D3 and B3LYP*) and large STO-TZ2P basis sets. The four ligands include a true corrin with a linear 14-p-electron conjugation pathway, a tetradehydrocorrin and an octadehydrocorrin with more extended, 2D conjugation, and a 5,6-dihydrocorrin with a shorter, linear 12-p-electron conjugation pathway. The calculations indicate that while both a true corrin and 5,6-dihydrocorrin can stabilize Co(I), only the latter stabilizes a Ni(I) ground state. In contrast, tetradehydrocorrin and octadehydrocorrin appear to exhibit a preference for M(II)-corrinoid(•2-) states (for charge-neutral complexes involving Co, Ni, and Cu). The unique ability of 5,6-dihydrocorrin to stabilize Ni(I), and thereby mimic cofactor F430, appears to be attributable to two factors: a modest expansion of the macrocycle’s N4 core brought about by saturation of the C5-C6 bond and a shorter conjugation pathway, which results in a relatively higher-energy p-LUMO (thereby averting ligand-centered reduction). Overall, the results help reconcile apparently conflicting findings on whether corrinoids can stabilize Ni(I).

item.title: Preserving Identity in an Ecosystem of Synthetic Cells by Macromolecular Crowding
item.description: To synthesize life from non-living matter, we require, at a minimum, ecosystems of synthetic cells that are capable of adaptive evolution. Such evolution, in turn, requires distinct individuals in an ecosystem to compete for resources so that successful ones can pass on their genotypes, while weaker ones succumb. Fuel-dependent synthetic cells built from complex coacervate droplets offer a route towards such evolution: they emerge when fuel is present, decay when it runs out, and freely exchange nutrients and waste with their surroundings. Moreover, because they lack a membrane, they readily take up molecules from their surroundings, negating the need for transmembrane pumps and channels. However, their membrane-less nature comes with downsides—when two droplets collide, they can fuse and pool their contents, erasing the differences between individuals that selection acts on. With a high fusion rate, an ecosystem with many individuals rapidly becomes a homogeneous pool of a few. To overcome that problem, we show that poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), an inert macromolecular crowder, suppresses fusion, allowing synthetic cells with distinct genotypes and phenotypes to coexist and compete within a single population. Crucially, the crowder does not accumulate in the droplets, leaving their interior chemistry untouched. Instead, the crowder reduces how often droplets collide and, more importantly, more than halves the chance that a collision ends in fusion. It does so through a combined effect of reduced interfacial tension and slower diffusion in the surrounding dilute phase, thereby making droplets more resistant to coalescence. For the first time, we can subject an ecosystem of fuel-dependent droplets with individual model identities to multiple fueling-starvation cycles and find that their identity is preserved. We show that crowding agents are a simple, broadly applicable tool for preserving the individual identity of membraneless synthetic cells, a prerequisite for their Darwinian evolution.

item.title: Isosteres in Chemistry
item.description: Dating back to 1919 with its coinage by Irving Langmuir, isosterism has continuously evolved over the past century. While ever changing, the overall idea has remained constant; isosteres are interchangeable groups or atoms which modulate a compound’s chemical properties. At a fundamental level, understanding the key concepts of isosterism has allowed for the development of a framework which enables intellectual compound design. As the undercurrent of all chemical innovation is the drive to discover, synthesize, or improve compounds such that their implementation improves their desired uses, isosteric rationale has been adopted by all areas of chemistry. However, the extent of intentional isosteric reasoning varies drastically across fields. While booming to popularity within the medicinal chemistry field with the creation of the bioisostere subcategory of isosterism, other fields like physical, inorganic, materials, and agricultural chemistry rarely attribute compound design changes to isosterism. In this review, we will cover the conceptualization and evolution of the term isosterism, provide an update on current medicinal chemistry application of isosteres, and highlight both intentional and unrecognized implementation of isosterism outside of the medicinal field. In both medicinal and non-medicinal chemistry applications, the effect of isosteric replacements will be emphasized. This collation of the wide range of isosteric replacements elucidates the breadth of applicability of the isostere concept with an aim of demonstrating how this inherently broad concept offers the potential to improve compound design across all areas of chemistry.

item.title: Reversible photoinduced excimer-like emission in indolocarbazole- derivatives in frozen solutions and host matrixes
item.description: Excimer formation can profoundly affect the emission colour and efficiency of organic optoelectronic devices, yet the mechanisms governing the formation and stability of intermolecular emissive states remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate irradiation-induced changes in the photoluminescence of indolo[3,2,1-jk]carbazole (ICz) and nitrogen-containing ICz derivatives in 2-methyltetrahydrofuran glasses at 77 K and in host–guest films at room temperature. Repetitive pulsed excitation causes a progressive increase in a broad, red-shifted emission band, accompanied by a decrease in monomer-like fluorescence. The magnitude and rate of this spectral evolution depend on the molecular structure, excitation fluence, accumulated number of laser pulses, emitter concentration, and local host environment. Melting and refreezing the frozen solutions restore predominantly monomer-like emission, demonstrating the reversible character of the photoinduced spectral changes. In host-guest films, the low-energy emission induced by ultraviolet irradiation can be similarly substantially suppressed by solvent-vapor annealing and regenerated upon renewed pulsed irradiation. These observations are attributed to an irradiation-induced redistribution of metastable local molecular configurations, which enhances intermolecular electronic interactions and promotes excimer-like emission. The results demonstrate that the excitation history of an organic material can alter the balance between monomeric and intermolecular emissive pathways, revealing a potentially important mechanism affecting the spectral stability and operational performance of organic light-emitting materials and devices.

item.title: GENESIS: Potency-Graded Contrastive Learning for Generative Molecular Design and Drug Repurposing in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
item.description: Computational drug discovery typically binarizes bioactivity, discarding the graded doseresponse signal needed for lead prioritization. We introduce Potency-Graded Contrastive Learning (PGCL), projecting frozen molecular language-model embeddings into a 128dimensional space via an ordinal contrastive objective, six-tier negative taxonomy, and tier-margin ranking. Across three seeds, PGCL achieves Spearman ρ = 0.555 ± 0.003 for potency ordering and target-switch AUROC = 0.967, outperforming flat-contrastive and binaryclassification ablations and roughly doubling ECFP4 activity-cliff discrimination. Among six generative architectures, our reinforcement-learning method CRAVE (Contrastive Reward-Aligned VAE Exploration) significantly exceeds non-RL baselines on OSCC potency after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.016). The frozen model transfers to lung adenocarcinoma without retraining — strongly along the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis (PIK3CA ρ=0.688, MTOR ρ=0.614, AKT1 ρ=0.583, EGFR ρ=0.561) but only modestly when pooled across all 16 LUAD-relevant targets (ρ=0.207, n=52,373). An integrated docking, ADMET, network-pharmacology, and leadoptimization pipeline screens 23,308 repurposing candidates, prioritizing 46 Tier-1 candidates, including 13 triple-validated elite compounds, with transparently reported safety pass rates (14.6%) traced to an EGFR/aniline training-corpus skew. The pipeline runs end-to-end on consumer-grade hardware, with code and protocols enabling transfer to other cancers.

item.title: From Rotor to Motor: An Experimental Guide for Light-Driven Directional Rotation
item.description: Research on molecular motors continues to expand as increasing attention is devoted to dynamic and out-of-equilibrium chemical systems. Among the different classes of artificial molecular machines, light-driven motors are the most extensively present, yet the fundamental principles governing their directional motion remain difficult to disentangle, particularly for non-specialists. This work applies these concepts in a workbook setting by gradually implementing molecular features to a base scaffold that turns it from a bistable system into an experimentally observable light-driven molecular motor. In doing so, it demonstrates how directional bias emerges as soon as relaxation of a high-energy state is coupled to a mechanical movement (a power stroke), while the motor performance can be addressed through modification of the underlying energy landscape. In addition, we show a practical workflow for benchmarking new motor candidates along with the experimental determination of their kinetic and thermodynamic parameters. To complement this study, we provide procedures for undergraduate students to synthesize and operate a molecular motor in practical courses.

item.title: Water-Enabled Organic Hydrogenation at Mg-Ni/Co Interface
item.description: Catalytic hydrogenation conventionally relies on precious-metal catalysts such as palladium and platinum together with compressed hydrogen gas, creating cost, safety, and operational constraints. Here we report a hydrogenation platform assembled in situ from abundant metal salts (Ni and Co) and magnesium, generating dynamic metal-magnesium interfaces under ambient conditions. Magnesium in the presence of chlorotrimethylsilane (TMSCl) reduced 2 salts of Ni and Co to generate a metal (Ni/Co) coated-magnesium, which activates water as the hydrogen source, enabling efficient hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes at room temperature without external hydrogen. Mechanistic studies support cooperative interfacial O-H bond cleavage and hydrogen transfer. This work elevates water to a practical reagent for reduction and introduces dynamic interfaces as a blueprint for sustainable catalysis.

item.title: Interfacial Transition-Metal Reduction, Surface Oxygen Depletion and LiNbO3 Protection in NCM622/Li6PS5Cl Cathodes Resolved by In Situ Nanoscale XPEEM
item.description: Degradation at the cathode-solid electrolyte interface limits high-energy-density sulfide-based allsolid-state batteries. For Ni-rich LiNi0.6Mn0.2Co0.2O2 (NCM622), cathode surface reduction and electrolyte oxidation are coupled through interfacial (electro-)chemical reactions. Although LiNbO3 coatings are known to mitigate interfacial resistance growth, their effect on this coupling during operation remains unclear. Here, we combine operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and in situ X-ray photoemission electron microscopy (XPEEM) to follow the chemical evolution of the NCM622 surface and interfaces with Li6PS5Cl (LPSCl) with depth sensitivity and nanoscale spatial resolution. Already at open-circuit potential, reduced transition-metals, oxygendeficient domains and sulfate species co-localize where NCM622 particles contact LPSCl. Upon high-voltage charging, electrochemically inactive Ni2+, Co2+, and Mn2+/3+ species become enriched at these contact regions, while oxygen depletion propagates inward across the particle surface. The LiNbO3 coating suppresses transition-metal reduction, improves surface electrochemical activity by increasing surface Ni and Co oxidation and confines oxygen depletion to the contact regions. Residual degradation nevertheless persists, consistent with inhomogeneous LiNbO3 coating coverage and its partial decomposition at high voltage. These findings provide nanoscale insight evidence that cathode and electrolyte degradation are interdependent and coupled through oxygen activity at the cathode surface and that effective coatings must suppress the cathode surface degradation.

item.title: Dynamic Aggregation as a Widespread and Reversible Mechanism of Capacity Fade in Aqueous Organic Flow Batteries
item.description: Aqueous organic redox flow batteries (RFBs) promise inexpensive large-scale energy storage for electricity produced from intermittent renewable energy. However, high capacity fade rates in RFBs that use inexpensive redox-active organic molecules (ROMs) represent a major barrier to commercialization. Most capacity fade mechanisms have been attributed to molecular decomposition of ROMs, and their prevention through molecular engineering typically raises the cost of the final battery system. Molecular aggregation and precipitation distinct from these molecular decompositions have been treated as a static, concentration-dependent consequence of the solubility of the ROMs in the electrolytes, affecting the performance of RFBs. Here, using NMR, UV-vis, microelectrode CV and comparative cell cycling, we introduce aggregation as a dynamic, non-covalent capacity fade mechanism in dihydroxyanthraquinones (DHAQs) as model compounds, that develops continuously over days to weeks at every concentration tested for certain flow battery electrolytes. Using reactive (ReaxFF) molecular dynamics and DFT calculations, we identify π stacking of the aromatic cores as the driving interaction accompanied by desolvation and favorable reorganization of the interfacial water network. Association is weakened by electrostatic repulsion between the anionic DHAQs but facilitated by the K+ counterions of the KOH supporting electrolyte, which screen this repulsion and occasionally bridge DHAQ molecules. Without further molecular modification, we demonstrate that mechanical agitation is a viable, broadly applicable route to recover this capacity loss and/or enable higher energy densities, reducing fade rates across structurally diverse ROMs including anthraquinones, viologens, and phenazines. For example, the capacity fade rate of 1,5-DHAQ decreased from 1.11% per day to 0.04% per day, about 28 times improvement in the stability of the electrolyte. The strategy introduced in this study enables the technology to reconsider the low-cost ROMs that have been discarded or neglected due to their high capacity fade rates and/or low solubilities, thereby easing the industrial development of economically viable organic RFBs for grid storage.

item.title: Solvent-Mediated Heat-Shock Trapping of Aromatic Carbonyl Guests in Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) Enables White-light Fluorescence, UV and Green-Light-Excited Red Phosphorescence, Delayed NIR Emission
item.description: Nonequilibrium polymer processing provides a route to generating emissive states without the need to synthesize new covalent chromophores. We report a simple physical method for encapsulating aromatic carbonyl guest molecules within the carbonyl rich polymer poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP). The resulting host-guest systems display guest dependent fluorescence across the visible region with a white light emitting complex being observed for one of the host/guest combinations with CIE coordinates (0.3147, 0.3244), close to the D65 daylight standard and a CCT of approximately 6430 K. Of the naphthalene derivatives investigated, 4-bromo-1,8-naphthalic anhydride (4-BrNA) displays a very different photo-physical behaviour when encapsulated in the polymer. It gives rise to red room temperature phosphorescence at 613 nm upon excitation at either 360 nm or 500 nm. Control experiments show that the emissive state is only obtained via solvent induced heat shock processing and not simply by dispersing the guest in the polymer. Co-trapping of the NIR emitter IR-783 with PVP/4-BrNA in the polymer leads to delayed near-infrared emission at 824 nm upon excitation at 360 nm, indicating that the emitter is being sensitized by the persistent donor reservoir. This is a rapid, metal free and modular approach which provides a process defined platform for white light fluorescence, visible light excited RTP and time gated NIR emission.

item.title: Electric Field-Driven Transitions from Nonclassical to Classical Carbonyls
item.description: Effect of external oriented electric field (OEF) is studied on the chemical bonding of isolated and complexed CO molecules using Density Functional Theory (DFT). Our findings, discussed the course of blue-shift and red-shift during the application of parallel and anti- parallel OEFs, with respect to the C–O bond vector, in isolated and complexed CO molecules. We give answer to a question, ‘Why the influence of electric field is more prominent in causing the red-shift than the blue-shift?’, via the detailed discussion of involved donor-acceptor interactions. Moreover, it is shown with suitable case studies that OEF can switch between classical and nonclassical carbonyl complexes.

item.title: Analysis of Halloysite Nanotubes as Nucleating Agents in Chain-Extended Recycled PET Foams
item.description: Halloysite nanotubes (HNTs) are reported as nucleating agents for crystallization and foam cells, but they have not been studied in recycled poly(ethylene terephthalate) (rPET) foams. Two grades differing in surface area (HNT1: 65 m2/g; HNT2: 25 m2/g) and Fe2O3 content (0.14 vs. 1.1 wt.-%) are compounded at 0–1.5 wt.-% into rPET chain-extended with 1 wt.-% Joncryl ADR 4468. Both grades reduce the isothermal crystallization half-time by up to 62 % at an almost unchanged Avrami exponent (n ≈ 2.3–3.0). However, the complex viscosity drops up to eightfold and reaches the terminal regime, indicating that HNTs modify the branched matrix through chain scission or chain-extender consumption. Relating crystallization to melt viscosity shows that this matrix modification dominates the acceleration, while heterogeneous nucleation contributes only at constant viscosity. In supercritical CO2 batch foaming (240 °C, 150 bar), foam density remains at 51–66 kg/m3 up to 0.25 wt.-% but rises to 246–328 kg/m3 at 0.5 wt.-%. At higher contents, HNT1 foams collapse, whereas HNT2 foams remain cellular owing to their higher melt viscosity. With a nucleation density close to the reference, untreated HNTs therefore nucleate crystals but not foam cells, as the viscosity loss outweighs any nucleating effect.

item.title: Population-Balance Tilt Sampling for Gradient-based Free-Energy Reconstruction
item.description: Gradient-based free-energy surface (FES) reconstruction typically faces a trade-off between the complexity of evaluating instantaneous forces and the systematic bias introduced by local asymmetry in position-based estimators. To overcome these limitations, we introduce population-balance tilt sampling (PBTS), an adaptive method that applies a linear tilt to a symmetric restraining potential and determines the central free-energy derivative by finding the tilt root that equalizes sample populations across the window center. Because the underlying molecular and symmetric restraining potentials cancel across tilt states within each window, cumulative multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR) reweighting depends exclusively on collective-variable displacements and tilt coefficients—enabling full trajectory reuse without instantaneous-force evaluations or potential-energy recalculations. Formulating a unified theory of odd-observable estimators to compare sign-based population balance against distance-based mean balance, we prove via moment inequalities that population balance guarantees a lower leading-order finite-window bias under cubic asymmetric perturbations. Furthermore, it bounds the influence of tail outliers on slope estimation while incurring only a modest increase in asymptotic variance. Applications to the Wolfe–Quapp model and gas-phase alanine dipeptide demonstrate accurate gradient extraction and robust FES reconstruction in one and two dimensions. Beyond free-energy estimation, the window-wise cumulative root histories native to PBTS act as parameter-free local convergence probes, uncovering hidden sampling bottlenecks and metastable branching along slow orthogonal degrees of freedom that are otherwise masked by global integration smoothing.

item.title: A Convenient One-Pot Route to [Thianthrenium][B(C6F5)4]
item.description: One-electron oxidants paired with weakly coordinating anions are indispensable for accessing reactive cations. The thianthrenium radical cation, [TA]•+ (TA = thianthrene), is a strong outer-sphere oxidant (E1/2 ≈ +0.7 to 0.8 V vs ferrocene/ferrocenium) whose neutral byproduct is easily removed, and its [B(C6F5)4]– salt (1) has been used in organometallic, rare-earth, and porphyrin chemistry. Existing preparations often rely on nitrosonium oxidation or salt metathesis in liquid SO2, which is challenging to handle, or MeCN, where traces may be deleterious to subsequent reaction steps. Here, 1 is obtained in one step at room temperature from AgI[B(C6F5)4], TA and 0.5 equivalents of I2 in CH2Cl2 or fluorobenzene (FPh); AgII is removed by filtration, and crystalline 1·CH2Cl2 and 1·0.5C6H5F are isolated in high yield on a gram scale.

item.title: ReConLiG: Reaction-Guided Design of Organometallic Ligands via Decoupled Generative Pretraining and Contrastive Alignment
item.description: Ligand design remains a central challenge in organometallic catalysis. Existing generative models rely on predefined molecular descriptors or require extensive labelled data for reaction-specific fine-tuning. We introduce ReConLiG, a framework that uses reaction information directly to generate ligand candidates without predefined target descriptors. ReConLiG decouples ligand generation from reaction guidance. The generative module learns a continuous and chemically interpretable ligand latent space from 500,000 unlabelled Sadphos pseudo-ligands. The reaction-guidance module uses contrastive learning to map reactions to ligands from 230 literature records covering 47 reaction classes. On 2,067 validation records, ReConLiG achieves a Top-5 hit rate of 93.3%. Generated ligands show a mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.82 to the experimentally preferred ligands, compared with 0.29 for a directly fine-tuned conditional decoder. A proof-of-concept extension to five general-ligand scaffold families demonstrates applicability beyond the Sadphos space. Across four Au-, Ir-and Pd-catalysed reaction scenarios, including three literature-level leave-one-out validations and one prospective unseen Pd Heck-type reaction, tested recommendations give yields of 70–99% and selectivity up to 94% ee or greater than 20:1 d.r. ReConLiG provides a practical and data-efficient route to reaction-guided ligand generation.

item.title: Thorium and Uranium bis- and tris-Tetraalkylphospholide Complexes
item.description: Phospholides are phosphorus-containing analogues of cyclopentadienides and softer p-donor ligands, but their actinide chemistry remains underdeveloped. We report the first thorium complexes of the tetraalkylphospholides TMP ({PC4Me4}–) and TEP ({PC4Et4}–): the tris(phospholide) complexes [ThIV(PC4R4)3X] (R = Me, Et; X = Cl, Br), together with their uranium(IV) analogues [UIV(PC4R4)3Cl]. To access the bromide complexes, we developed a simple route from thorium nitrate to [ThIVBr4(1,4-dioxane)2] and [ThIVBr4(THF)3] that does not require thorium metal and found that 1,2-dimethoxyethane is cleaved under related dehydration conditions with both bromide and chloride complexes. We isolated bis(phospholide) uranium(IV) dichlorides [UIV(PC4R4)2Cl2] (R = Me, Et), but not their thorium counterparts, as ligand redistribution gave mixtures containing tris(phospholide) complexes. Reactions of UIVCl4 with KTEP also gave dimeric uranium(III) complexes by adventitious reduction, with the product depending on the solvent. KC₈reduction of [UIV(TMP)3Cl] did not give [UIII(TMP)3], as analogous cyclopentadienide chemistry would suggest; instead, KCl was retained in a dimeric uranium(III) complex wherein one phospholide bridges uranium and potassium. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction shows longer metal–ring distances in the tris(phospholide) complexes than in cyclopentadienyl analogues, consistent with weaker p-donation, and variable-temperature magnetometry is consistent with the uranium(IV) and uranium(III) assignments.

item.title: eRoboChem: Autonomous Electrosynthesis Across Redox Modes and Reactor Designs
item.description: Synthetic electrochemistry offers powerful opportunities for molecular synthesis, yet its broader adoption remains hindered by the complexity of electrochemical reaction development. Beyond conventional reaction parameters, electrosynthesis requires careful choice of electrode materials, reactor designs and control of electron transfer, creating a complex experimental and optimisation challenge that can deter many synthetic chemists. Here, we introduce eRoboChem, a modular self-driving laboratory that integrates automated experimentation, analytical feedback and Bayesian optimisation across complementary flow and batch electrochemical reactors. Its versatility is demonstrated through three transformations spanning paired, oxidative and reductive electrosynthesis, each presenting distinct experimental challenges. Fully closed-loop flow operation enables autonomous reaction optimisation while accommodating gas evolution, whereas a complementary human-in-the-loop high-throughput batch module addresses electrode passivation and facilitates electrode screening. Systematic comparisons with conventional optimisation strategies, including one-factor-at-a-time and design of experiments approaches, demonstrate the value of Bayesian optimisation for navigating complex reaction spaces and extracting chemically meaningful and complementary insights. By adapting the experimental architecture to the requirements of the chemistry, rather than constraining the chemistry to a fixed reactor design, eRoboChem establishes a flexible framework for autonomous electrosynthesis and represents a step towards making electrochemical methodologies more accessible to the broader synthetic community.

item.title: Programmed switching gives multiblock copolymers of uniform composition
Diabat 2.0: A Comprehensive Diabatization Toolkit for Multichromophoric Systems
item.description: The construction of physically meaningful quasi-diabatic states and the evaluation of their electronic couplings are essential for describing nonadiabatic processes in molecular aggregates and other multichromophoric systems. Existing software implementations, however, are often restricted to dimers, two-state models, or particular types of quasi-diabatic states. Here, we present Diabat 2.0, a comprehensive toolkit for multistate diabatization in multichromophoric systems. It constructs the adiabatic-to-diabatic (ATD) transformation based on the adiabatic-state wave functions and energies obtained from external quantum chemistry calculations, yielding quasi-diabatic states and their electronic couplings in a nearly black-box manner. Diabat 2.0 implements several advanced ATD methods, including a general approach that can reliably construct quasi-diabatic states with diverse charge and excitation distributions without prescribing state types. This enables Diabat 2.0 to support diabatization in a broad range of scenarios that involve not only conventional charge-transfer, locally excited, and correlated triplet pair states, but also a variety of exotic states, such as mixed radical-triplet states, trion states, radical-coupled triplet-pair states, and charge-localized dicationic states. These capabilities are demonstrated in applications to several multichromophoric systems that pose substantial challenges to existing software.

item.title: (Arylsulfonyl)acetonitrile as an Efficient Unified Reagent for the Photocatalyzed Hydrosulfonylation of Alkenes
item.description: We report the organophotocatalyzed hydrosulfonylation of alkenes using (arylsulfonyl)acetonitriles (AACN) as a unified reagent acting both as a sulfonyl radical precursor, via photocatalytic C-S bond cleavage and as an intrinsic hydrogen-atom donor. This strategy expands the sulfonyl radical toolbox, offering broad substrate scope and enabling efficient synthesis of structurally diverse sulfones with excellent functional group tolerance.

item.title: Metastable Olivine-Type Intermediates in Maricite NaFePO4 Cycling Revealed by Operando XRD and DFT
item.description: NaFePO4 (NFP) is a potential cathode material for sodium-ion batteries and exists mainly as the maricite and olivine polymorphs. Maricite NaFePO4 (m-NFP) is the thermodynamically stable and synthetically accessible polymorph of NaFePO4, with a theoretical capacity of 154 mAh g-1 but is expected to exhibit limited electrochemical activity due to the absence of continuous Na-ion migration channels in its crystal structure. Its reported electrochemical activity has been attributed either to amorphization or to crystalline reconstruction, and previous computational studies have modelled desodiation within the known maricite and olivine polymorphs separately. It has therefore remained unknown whether desodiation of m-NFP crosses polymorph boundaries, and if so, through which intermediate. Here, we combine operando X-ray diffraction (XRD) with density functional theory (DFT) calculations to resolve this pathway. Operando XRD shows that m-NFP retains its long-range crystallinity during cycling, while systematic peak shifts and new reflections reveal an at least partially reversible crystalline transformation. A common convex hull of maricite-, olivine- and alluaudite-type NaxFePO4 (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) identifies alluaudite-type Na0.67FePO4 as the thermodynamically preferred intermediate. Calculated voltages exclude a maricite-retaining pathway but cannot discriminate between the remaining candidates. Pathway-resolved simulated XRD fingerprints, however, show that the experimental peak evolution is most consistent with a metastable olivine-type intermediate, lying only about 8 meV/atom above the hull, rather than with alluaudite. Structural similarity analysis indicates that this intermediate retains a more maricite-like local environment, suggesting that structural accessibility, not thermodynamic stability alone, selects the pathway. These results reconcile conflicting reports on m-NFP and show that the electrochemically accessed pathway of polymorphic electrode materials need not follow the lowest-energy intermediate.

item.title: A generative neural network architecture for structure elucidation
item.description: Determining molecular structure is central to chemistry. One-dimensional (1D) 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a standard technique in small molecule structure determination, but deducing a structure from these spectra remains challenging because of the vast chemical space involved. Deep learning models that predict structures directly from NMR data have shown potential in navigating this space, but are trained largely on simulated spectra and perform poorly on real experimental data. Here we present a transformer model trained purely on experimental NMR data from approximately 1 million molecules, which takes 1D 1H and 13C NMR peak lists together with molecular weight (readily obtained from mass spectrometry) and generates candidate structures as SMILES strings. On a held-out test set, our model identified the correct structure among 15 candidates for 56.6% of molecules with up to 19 heavy atoms (34.8% overall). On a benchmark of 86 experimental spectra, it was more than four times as accurate as the published NMR2Struct model at every candidate pool size, while generating more chemically valid candidates. Even when the exact structure was missed, its best candidates remained structurally close to the target, and its incorrect candidates retained many of the target’s functional groups, making them useful starting points for structure elucidation. These results demonstrate that training on experimental spectra substantially improves structure prediction from routine 1D NMR data.

item.title: Catalytic Activation of “Orbital-Symmetry-Forbidden” Pericyclic Reactions
item.description: Conservation of orbital symmetry imposes high barriers on formally forbidden pericyclic reactions, rendering such transformations inaccessible regardless of their thermodynamic driving force. A particularly compelling subset of such reactions involves the conversion of high-energy photoisomers. Although the catalytic activation of these and related orbital-symmetry-forbidden transformations has attracted increasing interest, the mechanistic understanding of how chemically different types of catalysts overcome orbital symmetry constraints has remained elusive. Herein, we report a systematic mechanistic investigation of the catalytic re-aromatization of Dewar-isomers of 1,2-dihydro-1,2-azaborinines employing three structurally and electronically distinct catalyst classes: classical Lewis acids, methylaluminoxane (MAO), and low-valent transition metal (TM) complexes. Combining variable time normalization analysis, 13C kinetic isotope effects, and DFT calculations, we demonstrate that these catalysts operate through mechanistically distinct yet electronically complementary modes of activation. In each case, the catalytic turnover converges on a common principle: circumvention of orbital symmetry constraints through electronic perturbation of the reacting π-system. We further provide the first mechanistic insights into MAO-catalyzed pericyclic reactions, shedding light on the reactivity of this complex and poorly understood structure. The mechanistic principles established for Dewar dihydroazaborinines extend to fundamentally different pericyclic manifolds, including retro-cycloaddition of a quadricyclane derivative, rearrangement of a benzvalene-type structure, and retro-electrocyclization of a diarylethene system. Combined, these findings establish a unifying mechanistic framework for the catalytic activation of orbital-symmetry-forbidden pericyclic reactions and offer guiding principles for the rational design of catalytic processes targeting formally forbidden transformations.

item.title: Benchmarking and Discovery of Ligands for Sterically Challenging Copper-Catalyzed C–N Cross-Couplings
item.description: Cu-catalyzed C–N cross-coupling has emerged as an attractive alternative to Pd-catalyzed methods from a sustainability point of view, yet ligand performance across sterically demanding substrate classes remains poorly understood. Herein, we report a benchmarking study of seven state-of-the-art ligands across 30 aryl halides and two representative amines to systematically evaluate steric effects in Cu-catalyzed amination. The substrate set includes aryl iodides, bromides, and chlorides bearing ortho substituents of varying steric and electronic demand, affording a dataset of nearly 500 reactions. The benchmarking study evaluated state-of-the-art ligands from the recent literature including those featuring 1,2-diarylated-1,2-diaminoarenes, hydroxypicolinamide, hydrazine, oxalamide, or benzilamide structural motifs. The resulting dataset provides practical guidance for ligand selection in discovery chemistry and reveals structure–reactivity trends governing the coupling of hindered substrates. This work led us to explore a broader set of ligands and conditions to enable the C–N cross-coupling of hindered substrates under conditions that avoid dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), a solvent associated with safety concerns at elevated temperatures in the presence of base. This led to the discovery of new ligands that are readily accessible from commercially available building blocks in ≤2 steps and perform well across a diverse range of ortho-substituted bromo- or chloro-arenes.

item.title: Natural fiber based natural rubber hybrid composites: Prospects and applications
item.description: Natural rubber (NR), derived from the Hevea brasiliensis tree, commonly referred to as the rubber tree, has been a crucial component in various industries for decades. The remarkable properties of NR, including its high elasticity, resilience, and exceptional mechanical strength, make it indispensable in the production of tires, seals, gaskets, medical equipment, and numerous other products. However, the growing focus on environmental conservation and the increasing demand for sustainable resources have increased interest in eco-friendly alternatives. One significant area of research involves incorporating biobased fillers into natural rubber composites. Scientists are investigating the use of renewable, non-toxic, and sustainable fillers within NR matrices to enhance material performance while reducing environmental impact. This chapter delves into the fabrication of biobased filler natural rubber composites, covering the types of fillers employed, their characteristics, modification techniques, and the potential applications of these innovative materials. Renewable natural resources, including plants, animals, and minerals, are the sources of biobased fillers. These materials function as reinforcement agents, improving rubber composite's mechanical, thermal, and environmental characteristics. Incorporating biobased fillers enhances the product's overall sustainability, lessening the reliance on materials derived from fossil fuels and decreasing the carbon footprint of the composites.

item.title: Measuring the Membrane Protein-Bound Lipidome
item.description: Lipids play diverse physiological roles in energy storage, signaling, and cell structure. Another less appreciated role is as allosteric modulators of membrane proteins. However, it is challenging to determine the identify and affinity of lipids interacting with a given membrane protein target. In this review, we discuss analytical advances in using lipidomics to profile lipids bound to specific membrane proteins, which we will refer to as protein-lipid interactomics. We will consider the challenges of solubilizing and isolating the membrane protein while retaining relevant lipid interactions, focusing on detergents and lipid nanoparticles made with polymer, peptide, and protein scaffolds. We will also discuss aspects of overall experiment design, including basic identification, quantitative experiments, progressive delipidation, and lipid exchange to probe the strength of lipid interactions. Finally, we conclude with key questions, current analytical challenges, and proposed future directions for this emerging field.

item.title: Diastereoselective synthesis of 3-monosubstituted phthalides through the MCR of phthalaldehydic acid, sulfoxonium ylides and thiols
item.description: A Brønsted acid-catalyzed multicomponent reaction (MCR) of phthalaldehydic acids, stabilized sulfoxonium ylides, and thiols is developed for the synthesis of 3-monosubstituted phthalides, a structural motif of considerable relevance to natural product and medicinal chemistry. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions and a ords the desired phthalide products featuring a thiol-functionalized side-chain in moderate to good yields with excellent anti-diastereoselectivity. The substrate scope encompasses di erent aliphatic thiols, sulfoxonium ylides, and substituted phthalaldehydic acids, although product stability during chromatographic purification limits isolated yields in some cases. In situ NMR monitoring reveals a two-step reaction pathway involving the rapid formation of a disubstituted sulfoxonium ylide intermediate, followed by slower product formation through a delayed catalytic cycle. The isolated intermediate also exhibits distinct reactivity toward other nucleophiles, enabling the synthesis of indole- and triazole-containing derivatives. Although enantioselective variants remain unsuccessful, the developed methodology provides an approach to structurally diverse phthalides of interest in natural product chemistry and o ers further insight into the mechanistic features of sulfoxonium ylide-based multicomponent reactions under Brønsted acid catalysis.

item.title: HFn-E2: a computationally designed human H-ferritin nanocage codelivering iron and the covalent GPX4 inhibitor ML210 for ferroptosis induction in lung cancer — design, PBPK scenario modelling, structure validation and human-data premise analysis
item.description: Ferroptosis induction by covalent inhibition of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) is a validated anticancer mechanism, but the most potent chemotype — the masked nitrile-oxide inhibitor ML210 — has never been formulated in a protein nanocage, and single-agent iron delivery is insufficient on its own. We present HFn-E2, a computationally designed human H-ferritin (HFn) cage intended to codeliver a mineralised iron core (target 1,000–2,000 Fe/cage) and ML210 (20–50/cage; Fe:ML210 ≈ 20:1–100:1) to transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1)-positive lung tumours, releasing both payloads upon lysosomal cage disassembly. The design combines a thermoresponsive-channel mutation (D44A) for thermal loading, a tHFn(+)-type endosomal-pH disassembly module (E61K/E64R with C-terminal truncationΔ160–182), and an optional MMP-cleavable shield reserved for a second version. A compartment PBPK scenario model, parameterised only from predecessor-formulation fits and literature anchors, predicts full-interval tumour coverage by free ML210 under all lysosomal-release scenarios, while the tumour:liver exposure ratio R reaches 0.60 in the realistic-best case and would require a ×8.34 tumour-uptake gain to reach 1.0 under honest liver accounting; MonteCarlo propagation (n = 1,000) gives R median 0.19–0.25 with P(R ≥ 1) ≤ 0.01, but coverage in 95.9% of draws. ESMFold structure validation anchored against two experimental structures (RMSD 0.62–0.71 Å) shows the engineered monomer within 0.36 Å of wild type, with no engineered site on the TfR1 contact surface. Human-data analyses (TCGA, DepMap 24Q4, UniProt) support the GPX4 dependency and MMP-9 premises, show GPX4 near-common-essentiality in lung lines (median Chronos−0.707,n=126), and — reported as found — do not support universal TFRC mRNA overexpression in lung adenocarcinoma. We also document a sequence discrepancy in the deposited tHFn(+) construct (PDB 9KAY carries E140K/E147K beyond the review-relayed definition). HFn-E2 is a fully computational design study with no experimental data; five pre-registered pilot experiments with frozen decision gates are defined to test it.

item.title: Selective Lanthanide-Binding Peptides: Molecular Insights into Binding Affinity and Selectivity
item.description: Rare earth elements (REEs), including the lanthanides, are essential to clean-energy technologies, semiconductors, electric vehicles, turbines, and other advanced materials that exploit their luminescent, magnetic, and catalytic properties. Current REE separation methods, however, suffer from poor selectivity, high solvent use, and environmental burden, which motivates greener and more selective strategies. Here we combine fluorescence binding measurements, molecular dynamics, enhanced-sampling calculations, descriptor analysis, and machine learning to determine how lanthanide-binding tag (LBT) peptides discriminate among trivalent REE cations in aqueous solution. The peptides operate in two binding regimes. For larger, lighter REEs, affinity is governed primarily by ion size, solvation, solvent accessibility, and non-bonded electrostatic interactions in a loosely coordinated binding pocket. For smaller, heavier REEs, the pocket contracts, and steric crowding, ligand–ligand electrostatic repulsion, and backbone torsional strain increasingly oppose further stabilization. Correlation analyses with sequence-derived, solvation, ligation, and conformational descriptors support this dichotomy. Analysis of selected LBT1-derived variants yields design rules: terminal charge tunes absolute affinity, ligating-residue geometry controls productive electrostatic coordination, a gatekeeper residue regulates water access and steric closure, and terminal residue hydrophobicity modulates amphiphilicity while preserving lanthanide-size sensitivity. Finally, classifiers trained on 37,041 sequences predict coarse Tb3+ affinity classes from a few bioinformatic descriptors, including disorder propensity, charge, amphiphilicity, and hydrophobicity, whereas predicting relative affinity across the full lanthanide series remains sensitive to solvation and binding-pocket remodeling. These results provide a molecular framework for engineering peptides for selective REE recovery and separation.

item.title: Nanogel structure shapes host-cell interactions and antibiotic performance against biofilm-associated and intracellular Staphylococcus aureus
item.description: Antibiotic treatment is often compromised by bacterial persistence within biofilms and host cells, contributing to recurrent infections and antimicrobial resistance.Here, a structurally diverse series of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM)-based nanogels (NGs) is evaluated to deliver ceftiofur (CF) against Staphylococcus aureus, using bovine mastitis as a clinically relevant context. Surface chemistry and network architecture are varied to determine how NG structure influences biological interactions and antibiotic performance. Although NIPAM-based NGs are not bactericidal, their composition modulates bacterial surface hydrophobicity and biofilm formation, as well as macrophage inflammatory responses and cellular uptake. CF-NG formulations exhibit strong activity against established biofilms and intracellular S. aureus, with all formulations reducing intracellular bacterial burdens by at least two log units. Cationic NGs enable CF to reduce viable intracellular bacteria to undetectable levels despite the lower cellular uptake observed for cationic NGs without CF. Anionic NGs provide the most balanced profile, combining favorable cytocompatibility, broad immunomodulatory effects, high uptake, and strong antibiofilm and intracellular activity. Overall, the results establish NG structure as a key determinant of interactions with bacteria and host cells and of CF-NG efficacy, providing design principles for nanocarriers targeting biofilm-associated and intracellular S. aureus.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: A 2% drift-tube window resolves skeleton length, not the PFOS isomers summed in serum
item.description: Suspect identification often treats two ions as one structure when their drift-tube collision cross sections agree within 2%. We asked what structural change that window can finish, pairing same-formula ions in the ToxCast drift-tube library, scoring each pair by the change in heavy-atom graph diameter, and treating each reported cross section as one draw with a 0.52 Å2 measurement scale. We then tested the rule against the ten measured perfluorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) isomers, the 89 PFOS connectivities in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency PFASSTRUCT list, the serum sum reported in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), and a travelling-wave library. The median absolute gap grew with the diameter change: 1.2, 1.8, 2.8, and 6.9 Å2 for zero to three bonds. Two percent of the linear PFOS cross section is 3.4 Å2, so a one-bond change stays inside the window and a three-bond change clears it. The measured PFOS isomers follow the same order: the monomethyls differ from linear by 1.3–2.9%, and the probability that the 5-methyl gap truly exceeds 2% is 0.70. Those monomethyls are the Sm-PFOS sum reported in NHANES (detected in 99% of people aged 12 and older; weighted median 30% of serum PFOS), and 33 of 36 branchversus-branch pairs agree within 2%, so mobility does not split the sum. Of 89 connectivities, 79 have no measured cross section, including a 36-member shell three bonds shorter than linear. A travelling-wave library did not reproduce the one-bond step. A 2% drift-tube window therefore reports a change in skeleton length rather than the methyl-position isomers that biomonitoring sums; cross sections for the unmeasured one-bond isomers and the three-bond shell would test the rule where it remains open.

item.title: Effect of Thermochemical Treatments on the Ethanol Yields from Taro Stalks
item.description: Taro stalks (Colocasia esculenta) were evaluated as a renewable lignocellulosic feedstock for bioethanol production. Three pretreatment methods—hydrothermal, dilute acid, and alkaline-peroxide—were used to release fermentable sugars. The effects of pretreatment solid loading (5–20% m/v) and sulfuric acid concentration (0.25–1.0% v/v) on hydrolysate fermentability were then assessed. While ethanol yields were comparable across pretreatments at 10% m/v solid loading, significant differences were observed in the total solids of the hydrolysates. Ethanol yield declined with increasing solid loading under hydrothermal and dilute acid conditions, and higher acid concentrations were associated with lower ethanol yields. Hydrothermal pretreatment at 5% m/v solid loading gave the highest ethanol yield (0.196 g/g dry biomass, from pooled replicates), equivalent to approximately 38% of the theoretical maximum calculated on a whole-dry-biomass basis. These findings suggest that taro stalks are a promising substrate for bioethanol production and underscore the importance of optimizing pretreatment conditions. Further studies are recommended to characterize hydrolysate composition and evaluate the economic viability of taro-based bioethanol systems.

item.title: Materials, manufacturing and sensing mechanisms of midinfrared photonic sensors
item.description: Mid-infrared (MIR) photonic sensors offer chip-scale access to molecular fingerprint spectroscopy for label-free detection of gases, chemicals, and biomolecules. Despite rapid progress in MIR materials, waveguides, resonators, sources and detectors, translating integrated MIR sensors into reproducible, calibrated instruments remains challenging. We examine how fabrication variability and component integration constrain the translation of device performance into reliable sensing. Materials and device architectures must preserve low optical loss, stable analyte access and compatibility with sources, detectors and packaging. This requirement is especially stringent in sensors, where exposed interfaces, suspended structures and high-overlap geometries make performance sensitive to sidewall roughness, surface chemistry and process variation. Here we review MIR photonics through the lens of sensing, with emphasis on material-platform trade-offs, manufacturability constraints and sensing mechanisms. By comparing sensing approaches using system-level metrics rather than isolated figures of merit, we show that no mechanism is universally optimal. The preferred choice depends on analyte phase, sampling geometry, spectral coverage, calibration robustness and integration pathway. Reproducible fabrication, applicationspecific integration and stable packaging emerge as central requirements for calibrated and fieldable MIR photonic sensors.

item.title: Methods for Expanding the NIST Mass Spectral Library with Highly Relevant Compounds
item.description: For over 40 years, the NIST Mass Spectral Library has served as the most authoritative source of reference quality mass spectra, used by thousands of labs to confidently identify chemical compounds. However, improvement of the library relies not only on expanding its size but also on increasing its relevance. To achieve this, a cheminformatic workflow was developed to facilitate the selection of chemical compounds that are maximally relevant across the numerous, often disparate disciplines and industries that rely on the library. At the crux of this workflow is a three-way optimization problem: acquiring the most relevant compounds, maximizing the number of compounds that can be purchased, and minimizing cost. To facilitate the evaluation of chemical relevance, the NIST Compound Ubiquity Index (CUbI) was created, which relies on 58 chemical catalogs selected to quantify the importance of each compound. This high-throughput approach to compound selection is critical to improving the NIST Mass Spectral Library’s relevance across many fields.

item.title: On parallel and sequential mass spectrometry
item.description: Many emerging frontiers in biological mass spectrometry, including comprehensive single-cell proteomics and ultra-low-input proteomics and metabolomics, are now constrained less by ion formation than by how efficiently instruments capture, route, and analyze ion flux from scarce and complex samples. In modern workflows, this flux is continuous and information-rich, yet only a fraction is recorded. As sample complexity rises, congestion and undersampling increase, lowerabundance species are preferentially missed, and information yield may plateau or even decline. Thus, the central bottleneck is increasingly one of instrument architecture. Early mass spectrometers separated ions in space rather than in time, continuously dispersing the primary ion beam with electric and magnetic fields and detecting ions at different locations on a phosphorescent screen or photographic plate. In this sense, they were truly parallel instruments, whereas modern instruments operate predominantly sequentially, processing, selecting, and measuring ions in successive time windows. Decades of refinement have brought remarkable gains in sensitivity and resolution, yet sequential acquisition still leaves much of the available ion population unmeasured. These considerations motivate a closer examination of what parallel and sequential operations mean in mass spectrometry. We propose a more rigorous definition of parallel mass spectrometry, distinguish physical parallelism from multiplexing, and consider which ion-handling and analysis steps can be performed concurrently and which remain intrinsically sequential. We also discuss how the balance between these modes is shaped by geometric and engineering constraints. Clarifying these distinctions provides a framework for evaluating existing and future instrument architectures and for identifying where parallelization may most effectively improve the speed, completeness and efficiency of mass spectrometric measurements.

item.title: LabSense: A Digital Workflow for Measuring and Reducing Resource Consumption in Research Labs
item.description: Laboratory science carries a disproportionately large environmental footprint, driven by intensive energy use, reliance on singleuse plastics, hazardous waste generation, and resource-heavy infrastructure, despite widespread desire among researchers to operate more sustainably. Yet many scientists lack the data needed to identify where to begin or which interventions would be most effective. To address this gap, we introduce LabSense, a modular, open‑source platform built on Raspberry Pi hardware that continuously monitors electricity consumption, water usage, fumehood operation, waste generation and chemical inventory in a typical materials chemistry lab. By transforming previously invisible behaviours and resource streams into real‑time, actionable data, LabSense enables evidence‑based decision making, behavioural change, and operational optimisation, providing a practical pathway toward data‑driven sustainable lab practice.

item.title: Structural and Electronic Origins of Ceria with Versatile Functionality: From Three-Way Catalysis to Chemical Mechanical Polishing and Actinide Surrogacy
item.description: With the rapid growth of the global rare-earth industry, high-abundance cerium-based functional materials, particularly CeO2 and its derivatives, have become essential in diverse applications, including automotive three-way catalysis, precision chemical-mechanical polishing, and actinide surrogate studies. However, the fundamental structural and electronic origins underlying the unique versatility of CeO2 remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a unified structure-electronics framework that links the geometric “mismatch” of Ce in the fluorite lattice with the energetic proximity of Ce 4f and 5d orbitals. We reveal that the slightly undersized cation/anion radius ratio of eight-coordinate Ce4+ in fluorite CeO2 (0.703 versus the ideal range of 0.732-1.0 for eight-coordinate binary oxides) serves as a geometric driving force for Ce4+ reduction to the larger Ce3+ state. The intrinsic stability of Ce4+ further enables facile Ce3+ reoxidation, establishing a dynamic redox equilibrium responsible for the reversible oxygen storage and release capability of CeO2. Meanwhile, the Ce 4f-5d energylevel overlap provides the electronic foundation for low-barrier Ce4+/Ce3+ switching, oxygenvacancy modulation, O2 activation, and tunable Ce-O bonding. This unified perspective rationalizes the multifunctionality of CeO2 in catalysis, interfacial bonding during chemicalmechanical polishing, and its role as an electronic analogue of f-d overlapping actinide elements such as U and Pu. Beyond elucidating the intrinsic chemistry of CeO2, this structureelectronics paradigm offers a general strategy for the rational design of next-generation ceriumbased functional materials.

item.title: Network Valence Dictates Gelation Pathway and Viscoelasticity in Reversibly Bonded TetraPEG
item.description: Theory predicts that reversibly bonded star polymers can undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) or form single-phase equilibrium gels depending on the polymer concentration and the bond equilibrium constant. To explore these possible phase behaviors, this work examines four-armed poly(ethylene glycol) star polymers (tetraPEGs) with transient boronate ester bonds and finds that they exhibit only a single-phase sol-gel transition. Bulk rheology shows that the bond equilibrium constant in the hydrogel, Kgel, is directly related to the sol-gel boundary. We develop a simple model combining Flory-Stockmayer network theory and bond thermodynamics, showing that the sol-gel boundary is largely determined by the tetraPEG overlap concentration c∗ and bond enthalpy ∆Hb. Excellent collapse of experimentally measured sol-gel boundaries for different tetraPEG arm lengths indeed occurs upon normalizing sol-gel concentrations by c∗. The model, in combination with simulations, explains why these tetraPEGs cannot access LLPS: a low Kgel results in a low average valence, or number of distinctly bound nearest neighbors, insufficient to drive LLPS. Going further, we determine a condition for Kgel to drive LLPS in four-arm star-polymer assemblies and find that the condition is consistent with the experimentally observed phase behavior of other 4-armed polymers. The concentration-dependent network valence, as estimated via Kgel, also explains experimental strain hardening in these materials. The framework presented here for understanding tetra-star networks lays the foundation for designing reversibly bonded stars with desired gel and phase-separation behaviors.

item.title: Spartan: Design and Recent Advances of a Molecular Modeling Program for Maximum Produc vity in Research and Educa on
Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Quillaic Acid, the Terpenoid Aglycone of QS-21
item.description: Quillaic acid is the aglycone of QS-21, a triterpenoid saponin that has been clinically evaluated as an immunoadjuvant. Current access to quillaic acid has so far been limited to isolation from natural sources or semisynthesis from minimally-oxidized oleanane precursors, which limits the range of modifications that can be performed on the pentacyclic skeleton. In the same vein, previous total syntheses of oleanane triterpenoids have largely relied on cascade polyene cyclization, which will be difficult to implement on quillaic acid due to its functional group arrangements. We disclose here a convergent annulation strategy to synthesize quillaic acid. Key features of the synthesis include a formal annulation of two key building blocks by way of Utimoto coupling and metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) cyclization, and generation of the A/B-ring fragment via enzymatic C–H oxidation of a dehydroabietic acid-derived precursor. The versatility of the route is further showcased through the synthesis of a novel analogue bearing a five-membered E-ring.

item.title: The Huc hydrogenase maintains catalytically active states in air using a high-potential iron-sulfur relay and internal electron transfer
item.description: Huc is a membrane-associated [NiFe]-hydrogenase that inputs electrons from trace levels of H2 into the aerobic respiratory chain of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Unlike most hydrogenases, Huc is catalytically active in air, yet it still can form the typically inactive Ni-B state. How it maintains catalytic turnover despite accessing this inactive state is unknown. Here, we use EPR spectroscopy to determine the oxidation state and relative reduction potentials of the metallocofactors in Huc. In contrast to canonical [NiFe]-hydrogenases, aerobically-isolated Huc contains active sites in their catalytic (Ni-C and Ni-L), turnover-competent (Ni-SIa and Ni-R), and inactive Ni-B states. Cryogenic illumination depletes Ni-B, a behavior without precedent in [NiFe]-hydrogenases, which we propose reflects electron transfer from a reduced iron-sulfur cluster that reductively reactivates Ni-B. Consistently, variable-temperature EPR spectra and dipolar simulations reveal strong electronic coupling between its three [3Fe-4S] clusters and an unusual redox organization in which the proximal and distal clusters remain oxidized while the medial cluster acts as an electron sink. This high-potential iron-sulfur relay favors electron transfer from the [NiFe] active site towards menaquinone while disfavoring reduction of O2. Thus, the observed selectivity against oxygen inactivation has a thermodynamic origin, offering guidelines for designing oxygen-tolerant catalysts for fuel oxidation.

item.title: ICPoly: An Automated Molecular Dynamics Workflow for Characterizing Structure, Dynamics, and Transport in Polymer Ion-Exchange Membranes
item.description: Predicting ionic transport in polymer ion-exchange membranes requires molecular models that connect polymer structure and hydration with local dynamics and collective charge transport. Here, we present ICPoly, an automated molecular dynamics workflow for characterizing the structure, dynamics, and ionic conductivity of these membranes. ICPoly integrates sequence-controlled polymer construction and fragment-based GAFF2 parameterization with staged classical and machine-learned equilibration, molecular-connectivity monitoring, and color-field nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD). Constant-field and constant-current formulations are implemented through modified Nosé–Hoover integrators in the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), while trajectory analysis characterizes the membrane structure and sulfonic acid deprotonation and predicts quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) spectra. The workflow is demonstrated for hydrated Nafion 212 in its proton and sodium forms using the reactive machine-learned UMA-s-1p2 potential. For representative Nafion-like fragments, UMA-s-1p2 achieves energy and force root-mean-square errors of 2.17 meV/atom and 41.84 meV/Å relative to density functional theory.
