The simulations reproduce the hydration-dependent decrease in density and reveal hydration-dependent changes in pore geometry and local organization, as well as incomplete sulfonic acid deprotonation. The two NEMD formulations yield similar velocity-based conductivity estimates. A displacement-based constant-field estimator shows faster apparent convergence but yields a substantially lower conductivity; it is adopted for subsequent calculations. Predicted proton and sodium conductivities increase with hydration, although proton conductivity is systematically underestimated and sodium conductivity is overestimated at low hydration. Overall, ICPoly provides a versatile and extensible computational framework that bridges polymer chemistry, molecular structure, dynamics, and ionic transport, enabling systematic investigations of structure–property relationships and facilitating the rational design of high-performance polymer materials.

item.title: Effect of Cu(II) Complexation on the Anticancer Activity of Zidovudine in the NCI-60 Human Tumor Cell Line Screen
item.description: Zidovudine (AZT, azidothymidine) was originally synthesized as a potential anticancer agent. Originally synthesized in 1964 by Jerome Horwitz at the Michigan Cancer Foundation during efforts to develop antitumor nucleoside analogues, AZT demonstrated insufficient anticancer activity in early evaluations and was not pursued further at that time. Despite its clinical success as an antiviral agent, AZT has continued to attract interest in its anticancer properties, including inhibition of telomerase activity, induction of DNA damage, modulation of cell-cycle progression, and disruption of survival signaling pathways. In the present study, AZT (NSC D-858683) and a Cu(II)-AZT complex (NSC D-858684) were evaluated by the National Cancer Institute Developmental Therapeutics Program using the NCI-60 human tumor cell line panel at a single concentration of 10 μM. AZT exhibited modest antiproliferative activity, producing a mean growth percentage of 98.27% and demonstrating its greatest activity against leukemia and myeloma cell lines. The CuAZT complex produced a similar mean growth percentage (96.05%) but substantially altered tumor selectivity, increasing the response range from 80.22 to 190.27 percentage units. The most notable finding was the emergence of enhanced melanoma activity. CuAZT produced net cell death in MDA-MB-435 melanoma cells (-61.63% growth) and reduced average melanoma growth from approximately 98.9% to 69.4%. These findings suggest that Cu(II) coordination modifies the biological response profile of AZT primarily through changes in tumor selectivity rather than through a substantial increase in overall potency. The distinctive activity profile of CuAZT supports future mechanistic studies and dose-response evaluation. Because Zidovudine (AZT) is still studied and utilized for specific retrovirus-linked cancers, although it is not a general-use chemotherapy drug for common solid tumors, using the 60 cell line panel provides insight to its efficacy against multiple types of cancer. In addition, our use of Cu(II) to improve the efficacy Taxol, raised the question if Cu(II) could do the same for AZT.

item.title: GPU-accelerated analytic Hartree–Fock gradients
item.description: Analytic nuclear gradients play a central role in quantum chemistry, enabling geometry optimization, ab initio molecular dynamics, and the generation of reference data for machine-learned interatomic potentials. Despite substantial advances in GPU-accelerated self-consistent field (SCF) methods, implementations of the associated analytic gradients on GPU remain comparatively less developed, often requiring as much computational time as the preceding SCF. Here we present a novel, high-performance GPU implementation of the analytic Hartree-Fock energy gradient in EXESS. The Coulomb and exchange gradients are evaluated by separate engines to exploit their markedly different sparsity. The exchange gradient retains the full eightfold integral symmetry through an in-kernel ring-buffer compaction that eliminates warp divergence. A hybrid Head-Gordon-Pople/Rys quadrature scheme, translational invariance and GPU-resident shell-pair batch construction further accelerate the evaluation.We benchmark the implementation on NVIDIA H200 GPUs across double- and triple-ζ basis sets, on molecules of up to 11,577 basis functions (ubiquitin). EXESS is the fastest code for every system and basis set tested, with average speedups over TeraChem (12.2x), GPU4PySCF (15.4x), cuEST (24.5x direct, 13.3x Grid-K), QUICK (222x) and VeloxChem (176x).

item.title: MolScrub: an open-source tool to generate conformers and protonate drug-like molecules
item.description: We introduce MolScrub, an open-source Python-based tool to prepare drug-like molecules for structure-based simulations. MolScrub takes common molecular input specifications like SMILES, predicts the protonation states, and generates 3D structures. It is a high-throughput tool, having an average runtime of 0.3 to 0.5 seconds per molecule per CPU core. MolScrub returns as few protomers and conformers as reasonable to avoid feeding high-energy states to downstream simulations. Protonation state assignment includes both pKa prediction for acid-base pairs and tautomer enumeration. During 3D-coordinate generation, MolScrub enumerates 6-membered ring conformations to ensure that the final structure is close to a global minimum. These improved input geometries benefit docking programs that do not change the internal state of small rings. MolScrub was primarily developed to generate high-quality ligand structures to support docking-based virtual screenings but its modules (pKa prediction, tautomer enumeration, and ring geometry corrections) can be used and configured independently to support other applications.

item.title: Patent Landscape of Gemini (Dimeric) Surfactants: Cationic Dominance in Intellectual Property versus the Emerging Green Surfactant Narrative
item.description: Gemini (dimeric) surfactants, molecules bearing two hydrophobic tails and two head groups joined by a spacer, have been developed across cationic, anionic, nonionic, zwitterionic, sugar-based, and amino acid-based chemistries over several decades. To the author's knowledge, this review is the first to combine a systematic patent landscape analysis spanning all major charge classes with a survey of current academic research trends to ask a direct question: Does patent activity track academic attention in this field? Drawing on 41 patent families listed in this review (Supporting Information S1) and over 20 peer-reviewed sources, the answer is no. Cationic quaternary ammonium gemini surfactants, driven mainly by enhanced oil recovery, corrosion inhibition, antimicrobial, and personal care applications, account for 25 of the 41 patent families identified here. In contrast, recent academic reviews describe amino acid- and sugar-based gemini surfactants, rather than cationic quaternary ammonium chemistry, as the field's emerging green surfactant direction; searches specifically for arginine- or lysine-specific gemini surfactant patents returned no on-point results. This review further documents a recurring definitional ambiguity between "two hydrophobic tails" and "two charge centres" in patent claim language, a near absence of true single-molecule zwitterionic gemini surfactants, and no agricultural or pesticide adjuvant application identified for any gemini surfactant charge type in either the patent or the academic searches. These findings identify several concrete, evidence-based directions for future synthetic, formulation, and intellectual property work.

item.title: GC-HRMS Workflow for Automated Chemical Analysis in Exposome-Wide Association Studies
item.description: The comprehensive characterization of the chemical exposome in large epidemiological cohorts requires high-throughput, reliable, and sensitive analytical pipelines. We present a scalable, fully automated workflow for liquid-liquid extraction coupled with gas chromatography-high resolution mass spectrometry (GC-HRMS), designed for simultaneous targeted and non-targeted exposomics. Suitable for large-scale studies, with a runtime of 25 min per sample that includes robotic sample preparation and data acquisition, this work describes an analytical framework to ensure high data quality in human biomonitoring and exposomics studies. It requires a low volume of biospecimen, 0.1 mL of plasma, and maintains compatibility with parallel LC-MS workflows for enhancing chemical space coverage. A rigorous quality control strategy was implemented, using the apparent recovery as a key parameter for evaluating performance in GC-HRMS. Isooctane was selected as the extraction solvent for yielding the highest overall apparent recoveries for a targeted panel of 106 persistent organic pollutants (PCBs, PBDEs, PCDDs, OCPs) and PAHs. The final workflow includes >180 anthropogenic compounds for which authentic reference standards potentially enable Level 1 identifications. Three approaches for sensitivity assessment were discussed, resulting in limits of quantification ranging from 0.2 to 2.0 ng/mL. Procedural calibration, with fortified biological samples and cohort-specific pooled QC samples, is proposed to effectively correct for matrix interferences and ensure accurate (semi-)quantification across analytical batches. The final analytical design confirmed the fitness-for-purpose of the automated-LLE-GC-HRMS pipeline. The integration of NIST SRM 1958 served as a benchmark for in-house long-term stability and inter-lab comparability. The potential of retrospective data analysis for emerging contaminants is demonstrated by non-targeted analysis (NTA) of commercially available pooled plasma and the two certified reference material SRM1950, and SRM1958. This scalable, standardized framework addresses limitations in sample availability while providing the reliability needed for exposome-wide association studies (ExWAS).

item.title: ExFiT: Ensemble-based Excited-State Character Fingerprinting across Temperatures
item.description: The character of electronically excited states, such as the balance between local excitation (LE), charge transfer (CT), and the spatial separation of electron and hole densities, strongly influences absorption properties and the electronic-state landscape at the Franck–Condon geometry of organic chromophores, evaluated at ground-state nuclear configurations. Conventional analyses based on single equilibrium geometries neglect thermal fluctuations that can significantly alter this character. We present ExFiT, an ensemble-based computational pipeline that interfaces with GPU-accelerated electronic-structure calculations for fingerprinting excited-state character across temperatures. ExFiT combines finite-temperature Wigner sampling with ensemble-resolved excited-state analysis and principal component analysis to quantify distributions of CT metrics, electron-hole separation, entanglement, and orbital participation. Application to representative chromophores (trans-azobenzene, (E)-hemithioindigo, para-nitroaniline, and coumarin 481) reveals distinct regimes of thermal behavior, ranging from robust excited-state character to broadened descriptor distributions and bright-state reordering associated with closely spaced excited states within the Franck–Condon ensemble. NTO overlap further shows that changes in optical brightness need not reflect changes in excited-state character, distinguishing state perturbation from state reassignment. These results demonstrate how thermal fluctuations modulate excited-state electronic structures and establish the applicability of ExFiT as a framework for generating statistically meaningful initial-condition ensembles for spectral simulations and future nonadiabatic dynamics studies.

item.title: Programmable Nanofluidic Confinement: From Static Nanotopographies to Reversible Electrokinetic Trapping
item.description: Single-molecule analysis increasingly relies on the ability to immobilize, confine, and manipulate biomolecules in solution. Nanofluidic devices provide a powerful route to this goal by using embedded nanotopographies on-chip to define free-energy landscapes that enable spatial manipulation, transport, confinement, and conformations that can be leveraged for biomedical applications. One classic example for molecular confinement is DNA extension in nanochannels, which has allowed for high-throughput genomic sequencing on-chip. Classic nanofluidic devices however are often limited by the static nature of their confinement landscapes, which are fixed by the static geometry of the device after fabrication, not allowing for real-time manipulation. Examples from optics (e.g. optical tweezers, optical lattices, holographic optical tweezers) demonstrate that, in principle, it is possible to achieve high-throughput dynamic control by using external fields to impose and alter confinement. In this review, we discuss different methods to engineer tunable free energy landscapes for nanoscale confinement of molecules. We first describe fabrication strategies and static nanofluidic geometries, emphasizing how top-down nanotopographies impose equilibrium molecular conformations. We then examine mechanically and pneumatically tunable platforms that modulate confinement after fabrication, followed by more tunable field-based approaches that use electrokinetic, thermophoretic, optical, and plasmonic effects to localize, concentrate, and manipulate molecules in solution. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies that combine lithographically defined nanofluidic arrays with externally applied fields to create reversible and dynamically tunable confinement landscapes. Such approaches point toward a new generation of nanofluidic devices in which single molecules can be immobilized, released, and driven between conformational states in real time, enabling high-throughput studies of non-equilibrium biomolecular dynamics and active molecular control on chip.

item.title: What makes a laboratory self-driving? Mapping the SDL terminology landscape and introducing the FLEx categorization framework
item.description: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are increasingly used to accelerate experimentation across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, and related fields. Yet, the rapid development of autonomous experimentation has produced a fragmented terminology landscape in which overlapping terms, including autonomous laboratories, materials acceleration platforms, and robot scientists, are applied inconsistently. This complicates comparisons between systems and obscures what constitutes scientific autonomy. Here, we examine the definitions, historical development, disciplinary associations, and usage patterns of SDLs and related concepts. We further review existing approaches to categorizing autonomous laboratory systems and show that many rely on characteristics such as hardware complexity, system architecture, or human involvement that are difficult to apply consistently across disciplines and technologies. To provide a technology-independent alternative, we introduce the Feedback Loop Extent (FLEx) framework. FLEx classifies systems according to how far experimental feedback reaches into the scientific process, progressing from scripted execution without a scientific feedback loop to parameter optimization, autonomous experiment planning, hypothesis formulation, and scientific goal formulation. Applying FLEx to representative published systems shows that most contemporary SDLs autonomously plan experiments within human-defined objectives, whereas few demonstrably formulate hypotheses and none unambiguously reformulate broader scientific goals. FLEx provides a common language for distinguishing automation from different forms of autonomy and enables more transparent comparison and reporting of current and future SDLs.

item.title: Configuration-dependent hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics on S-doped RuO2(110): A first-principles study
item.description: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a promising non-platinum electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet its intrinsic activity is limited by strong hydrogen adsorption on coordinatively unsaturated Ru surface sites.Density functional theory calculations show that substitutional sulfur doping improves the HER adsorption thermodynamics of RuO2(110) by tuning hydrogen adsorption via local environment engineering. S doping weakens excessive hydrogen binding and drives the system toward near-optimal HER thermodynamics, approaching the benchmark ΔGH of Pt[3]. Symmetry-based enumeration and energetic screening were used to construct 86 inequivalent S-doped RuO2(110) models, from which four thermodynamically accessible configurations with favorable hydrogen adsorption were identified. The results reveal that dopant concentration governs the thermodynamic accessibility of S-doped configurations, whereas the local atomic configuration around the Ru active sites determines the hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics within the accessible concentration window. Among the accessible motifs, the 2S-top H adsorption site (H on the Ru adjacent to a single S dopant) is the most favorable, with ΔGH ≈ 0.06 eV, essentially equal to the 1S-top site (0.06 eV). Electronic structure analysis shows that S-induced hybridization between Ru 4d and dopant-derived p states leads to a downward shift of the Ru d-band center and reduced charge localization, tuning the hydrogen adsorption free energy from −0.26 eV on pristine RuO2 to approximately 0.06 eV.

item.title: Multigram Synthesis of the 1,3-Substituted Cuneane Amino Acids
item.description: Cuneanes are obtained from cubanes in a single step and reproduce the exit vectors of meta- and parasubstituted benzenes, but the corresponding amino acid building blocks have remained unavailable. Herein, we report a preparative route to cuneane amino acids based on the Curtius rearrangement of cuneane halfesters. Both regioisomers of the 1,3-disubstituted series are accessible from the two complementary halfesters: tert-butanol gives the Boc-protected amino esters in 84% and 91% yield on a 10 g scale, and standard operations convert them into the Boc and Fmoc amino acids, the methyl and tert-butyl esters, and the corresponding amine hydrochlorides in 55-99% yield. In the 2,6-disubstituted series, the deprotected amine opens the cage: acidic removal of the Boc group gives the known ring-opened ketone, and removal of an allyl carbamate under neutral Pd(0) conditions gives the same ketone in 55% yield. Carrying out that removal in the presence of an active ester acylates the amine as it forms and delivers the benzamide in 54% yield.

item.title: Light-Induced Synthesis of Ultra Thick Polymer Brush Coatings with Boosted Antifogging Properties
item.description: Polymer brushes with thicknesses exceeding 500 nm are synthetically challenging and rarely reported, while their applications remain largely unexplored. A range of applications, including catalytic, antifriction, and antifogging/antifreezing surfaces, could greatly benefit from their highly packed and extended conformation. Very recently, ultra-thick (200–3000 nm) polymer brushes have been demonstrated with largely improved wear bearing in antifriction tests. Herein, we demonstrate eosin Y-mediated SI-PhotoATRP to generate poly(oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether)methacrylate (POEGMEMA) brushes up to 800 nm thick, easily tunable with green-light intensity. The series of polymer brushes ranging from 30 to 800 nm were systematically tested against fogging under cooling. The developed testing setup enabled detection of dew points, whose 2 shifts were most significant for the thickest POEGMEMA brushes, with a striking shift of 9 °C at 0.5 °C∙min−1. The analysis at different cooling rates enabled the decoupling of kinetic and thermodynamic components of the antifogging of polymer brushes for the first time. Our work exemplifies a synthetic route toward generation of ultra-thick polymer brushes and strongly supports their need for further structure-property relationship studies and potential applications.

item.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts
Linear-Algebraic Audit of Biomedical Matrices: Five Empirical Case Studies in Regularized Inference
item.description: High-throughput biomedical assays—ranging from gene expression microarrays to mass spectrometry and clinical registries—routinely exhibit severe rank deficiency (N ≪ P ), zero-inflation, and extreme sample outliers. Standard chemometric and bioinformatics pipelines apply variance auto-scaling, simplex normalization, and bilinear projections (PCA/PLS-DA) without verifying operator conditioning or modal localization. Grounded in inverse problem theory, this empirical study subjects five public biomedical datasets to a sequential four-step linear-algebraic audit evaluating residual Gram conditioning (κ), Effective Degrees of Freedom (DoF), singular spectra (Σ), and Participation Ratios (PR). Across five empirical regimes—Golub leukemia microarrays (72×7129), a large-scale oncology cohort (1545×10935), zero-inflated NCI Arcene mass spectra (200 × 10000), Pomeroy central nervous system tumor profiles (60 × 7129), and the Cleveland cardiology registry (270 × 13)—we demonstrate how uncalibrated preprocessing inflates background noise threefold, collapses leading components onto fewer than 7 outlier samples, and bends multi-batch artifacts into parabolic horseshoes. Removing just 0.6 percent of leverage outliers identified by PR restores sample coherence nearly ninety-fold (PR : 6.4 → 548.1), providing a rigorous diagnostic standard for biomedical data hygiene.

item.title: Towards a Metrological Validation of PFAS Property Predictions by In-Context LLMs Across Four Architectures
item.description: In recent years, the use of large-language models (LLMs) as prediction tools has become increasingly popular. Despite this popularity, the metrological validation of LLMs in the study of chemical problems has been somehow neglected to date. To illustrate this need in chemistry, we introduce a minimal, metrologically grounded framework for validating in-context learning (ICL)-based prediction in LLMs on molecular physicochemical properties with reliable estimation of uncertainty. Our framework integrates a multicycle testing protocol (Mc = 50 replicate cycles per model-property cell) with a six-metric bundle: central tendency (mean MAE over replicate cycles), reproducibility (interquartile range), regression performance (RMSE, and R2), information-theoretical lower bound on the amount of captured signal (𝐼" in nats), and ordinal 2 performance (accuracy against the median in the dataset), plus three cross-property and crossmodel comparison metrics: NRMSE, Welch’s z-test, and Scaling Law Fit exponents. We use this framework to validate four LLMs, two dense (8B and 70B parameters; 1B = 109) and two mixture-of-experts (MoE; 17B active parameters with 109B and 400B in total), for predicting eight per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) properties: boiling point (BP), melting point (MP), vapor pressure (VP), Henry’s law constant (HLC), octanol-water partition coefficient (LogKow), aqueous solubility (LogS), acid dissociation constant (pKa), and critical micelle concentration (LogCMC). In this benchmark, the frontier MoE model (Maverick 400B parameters) achieves a mean validation NRMSE of 14.4 %, and the mid-scale MoE model (Scout, 109B parameters) outperforms our larger dense model (Llama-3.3-70B) despite having 4.1× fewer active parameters. This suggests that MoE routed capacity can substitute for activeparameter scale in chemical applications of ICL. When compared to published QSPR and DFT baselines, LLM-ICL beats these approaches on three of eight directly comparable properties (pKa by 43 %, LogKow by 31 %, HLC by 10 %) and trails behind on five (BP, MP, LogS, VP by 12 % to 75 %, and LogCMC by a factor of approx. 3.3), despite using approximately 32 incontext examples (32 for seven properties, 20 for HLC) versus the training sets comprising 102 to 105 molecules used in these approaches. We also discuss a validation-set anomaly in the case of LogKow, where our mid-scale dense model Llama-3.3-70B outperforms the frontier MoE model on all four validation metrics, possibly due to better coverage of the pretraining data. Permutation (shuffled-label) and information-access blinding controls show that genuine structure-response signal is present, but that the native-prompt accuracy depends substantially on pretrained, property-specific knowledge and familiar target scales. Overall, our results suggest a two-fold conclusion on the competitiveness of LLM-ICL: it succeeds in predicting chemical

item.title: Self-Consistent Induced Dipoles for MACE-POLAR in Molecular Embedding and Classical Dynamics
item.description: We couple the native Gaussian multipoles of MACE-POLAR-1-M to classical induced dipoles and compare the resulting solute densities, fields and forces with quantum references. The density-driven fixed point has a nonzero energy derivative with respect to its dipoles. An adjoint recovers forces on the converged surface to within 2.13 × 10−7 eV/Å of reconverged finite differences in twelve force-test configurations. A separate density comparison treats both partners quantum mechanically at twelve geometries of six small complexes. At a common Gaussian width of 1.5 Å, enabling mutual induction changes the native MACE solute density by at most 6.81 × 10−4 𝑒 in integrated absolute difference. For water facing chloride at 3.15 Å, the density change is 0.000107 𝑒 with the MACE-induced dipole, 0.00426 𝑒 with the prescribed DFT-induced dipole, and 0.01026 𝑒 with DFT at that same dipole. Thus the error involves both the field that induces chloride and the water response to the returning field. For Na+–Ar at 6 Å, the predicted solute multipoles are unchanged, while environment induction gives an interaction of −9.19 meV, close to the classical induction limit

item.title: AMBER2LAMMPS: Validated conversion of AMBER-family topologies to LAMMPS
item.description: AMBER topology files encode a complete molecular-mechanics model rather than only molecular connectivity. Translating them to LAMMPS requires preservation of bonded parameters, charges, Lennard-Jones coefficients, exclusions, topology-specific 1–4 scaling, masses, and periodic-cell semantics. AMBER2LAMMPS is an open-source Python package that converts one or more fully parameterized AMBER topology templates and matching PDB coordinates to LAMMPS data and parameter files. The converter derives SCEE and SCNB scaling from active proper dihedrals, represents non-covalent GAFF2–GLYCAM mixtures with repeated hybrid pair-style instances, supports validated ff14SB, TIP3P, ion, and Li/Merz 12–6–4 cases, plus HMR mass mapping and TIP3P SHAKE initialization, and fails before output for unsupported combinations. Reproducible continuous-integration fixtures compare component energies and every Cartesian force against AmberTools sander. A command-line interface, Python API, and bounded Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface, with optional (CLI) or automatic (MCP) provenance, support both manual and automated workflows while keeping scientific decisions inspectable.

item.title: Informatics-Driven Chemputation within the HERA Framework: Mathematical Modeling of Molecular State Entropy, Reaction-Diffusion Flow Kinetics, and Closed-Loop Bayesian Optimization
item.description: The integration of physical chemical synthesis with digital information networks remains bottlenecked by the lack of unified frameworks for lossless molecular state serialization, secure long-range telemetry, and automated robotic re-materialization. This study introduces the HERA framework, a comprehensive model that converts chemical supply chains into executable digital information routing problems. We establish a rigorous information-theoretic foundation by defining total chemical state information entropy H(C) as a decomposition of structural discrete entropy (H_struct), thermodynamic vibrational entropy (H_vib), and compositional concentration entropy (H_conc). To bypass intractable high-scaling quantum mechanical calculations (O(N⁷) Coupled Cluster theory), we formulate Graph Neural Network (GNN) surrogate operators (H_GNN) that reduce computational complexity to O(N²) while bounding prediction error within ε_q <= 10⁷Hartree. Furthermore, we derive lossless HERA Data Container (HDC) compression bounds, reaction-diffusion transport kinetic partial differential equations governed by the Peclet number for continuous-flow Chemical Processing Units (ChemPUs), and Kullback-Leibler (D_KL) spectral divergence thresholds to enforce hardware safety and error-correction. Grounded in open analytical standards (mzML, nmrML, AnIML), chemoinformatics serialization (InChI, RInChI, xDL), and closed-loop Bayesian optimization within self-driving laboratories, HERA establishes a secure, dual-use protected pathway for decentralized pharmaceutical manufacturing, hazardous forensics, and deep-space astropharmacy.

item.title: Spacer accommodation under geometric confinement governs phase behavior in mixed Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson halide perovskites
item.description: Mixing organic spacers broadens the structural diversity of two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs); however, predicting whether chemically distinct spacers can be incorporated into a shared layered phase remains a significant challenge. Here, we integrate high-throughput compositional screening and diffraction-based phase mapping with molecular dynamics simulations accelerated by machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP-MD) to investigate combinations of five Dion–Jacobson (DJ) spacers with varying alkyl-chain lengths and three aliphatic or aromatic Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) spacers. Contrary to conventional structural-matching expectations, large differences in parent-phase interlayer spacings do not necessarily preclude spacer mixing, whereas smaller differences do not guarantee it. MLIP-MD simulations of locally mixed and phase-separated spacer configurations reveal a correlation between local d-spacing deviations relative to the parent DJ phase and experimentally observed phase behavior in aliphatic spacer combinations. The simulations further reveal that these trends arise from molecular accommodation within the geometric constraints imposed by the DJ framework, where RP and DJ spacers adapt their orientations and conformations to accommodate a shared interlayer geometry while preserving favorable intermolecular packing. Guided by these insights, selected mixed-spacer compositions that combine DJ interlayer bridging with RP conformational flexibility exhibit enhanced thermal and ambient stability, while mixed-spacer surface treatment of 3D HPs improves photovoltaic performance and thermal stability. Together, these findings establish molecular accommodation as a guiding principle for spacer selection beyond conventional structural matching, and provide a route toward predictive synthesis of layered HPs.

item.title: QM/MM Simulations Reveal Differences in Hydrolysis Mechanisms of Ertapenem and Faropenem in L1 Metallo-β-Lactamase Leading to Different Product Binding Modes
item.description: L1, a class B3 metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) from Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, efficiently hydrolyzes most β-lactam antibiotics and evades β-lactamase inhibitors, both clinically available and those in late-stage trials targeting other MBLs. Detailed understanding of the L1 mechanism is necessary to design effective inhibitors. Building on our previous quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) study of L1catalyzed hydrolysis of the penem antibiotic faropenem, we here investigate hydrolysis of a 1β-methyl carbapenem (ertapenem) using MM and enhanced sampling QM/MM MD simulations at the DFTB3 level, comparing the two mechanisms to understand the distinct product binding modes observed crystallographically. The geometry of the transition state for the first, amide bond cleavage, reaction step is similar for both substrates. However, differences are apparent in the subsequent proton transfer step, corresponding to the different binding modes observed crystallographically for the respective products. For faropenem, a bulk water molecule enters the active site, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product via rotation about the C5–C6 bond and protonation at position C2. For ertapenem, the metal-bridging hydroxide is the proton source, and the equivalent rotation is associated with a relatively high barrier. Instead, the more favorable rotation of the C6-carboxyl enables protonation at C2, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product in a distinct binding mode. Long-timescale MM MD simulations indicate rapid dissociation of the ertapenem-derived imine, compared to the faropenem-derived species, from the L1 active site, offering insight into the relative stability of these binding modes. These data reveal how carbapenem and MBL structure influence hydrolysis pathways, and may inform rational MBL inhibitor design.

item.title: A Convenient One-Pot Route to [Thianthrenium][B(C6F5)4]
item.description: One-electron oxidants paired with weakly coordinating anions are indispensable for accessing reactive cations. The thianthrenium radical cation, [TA]•+ (TA = thianthrene), is a strong outer-sphere oxidant (E1/2 ≈ +0.8 V vs ferrocene/ferrocenium) whose neutral by-product is easily removed, and its [B(C6F5)4]− salt (1) has been used in organometallic, rare-earth, and porphyrin chemistry. Existing preparations often rely on nitrosonium oxidation or salt metathesis in liquid SO2, which is challenging to handle, or MeCN, where traces may be deleterious to subsequent reaction steps. Here, 1 is obtained in one step at room temperature from AgI[B(C6F5)4], TA and 0.5 equivalents of I2 in CH2Cl2 or fluorobenzene; AgII is removed by filtration, and crystalline 1·CH2Cl2 and 1·0.5C6H5F are isolated in high yield on a gram scale.

item.title: Correlative Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy and Nano-DESI Mass Spectrometry Imaging for Mapping Isomeric Triglycerides in Lipid Droplets in Biological Tissues
item.description: Lipid droplets (LDs) are key organelles involved in lipid storage and metabolic regulation. Triglycerides (TGs) are the major component of LDs’ neutral lipid core. Alterations in TG composition are associated with different biological states or disease conditions, yet spatially resolved analysis of TG isomers in biological tissues remains challenging. Here, we present a correlative multimodal imaging strategy that integrates stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy with high-resolution nanospray desorption electrospray ionization (nano-DESI) isomer selective mass spectrometry imaging (iMSI) to map LD morphology and isomeric TG distributions in biological tissues. We performed SRS imaging on a type 2 diabetes (T2D) mouse liver tissue section to visualize individual LDs with sub-micron resolution and without the need of labeling. We then performed nano-DESI iMSI on the same tissue section. By optimizing nano-DESI solvent composition and tissue preparation conditions to favor formation of ammonium adducts of TGs, [M+NH4]+, we obtained simplified, isomer-selective MS2 fragmentation patterns revealing characteristic fatty acyl neutral losses. We then used these characteristic fragment ions to perform high-resolution iMSI of four TG species (TG 50:2, TG 50:3, TG 52:2, and TG 52:3) and map the spatial distributions of their isomers. Spatial correlation analysis across defined regions of interest demonstrated consistent signal trends between SRS-derived LD density and MSI TG ion signal, with both modalities showing minimal signal in blood vessel regions and elevated signals in LD-rich areas. This first demonstration of iMSI of TGs in biological tissues provides a framework for correlative SRS-MSI imaging of LDs and TG isomers in metabolic disease models.

item.title: Direct Access to 5-Aryl-2-Pyrones via Palladium-Catalyzed Decarbonylative Cross-Coupling of Coumalic Acid
item.description: The selective synthesis of 5-substituted 2-pyrones remains challenging despite their synthetic potential. Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed decarbonylative Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling of simple coumalic acid, providing direct access to 5aryl-2-pyrones in up to 58% yield. Enabled by DPEphos, the transformation accommodates diverse arylboronic acids while preserving the reactive heterocyclic framework. Subsequent cycloaddition chemistry exploits the localized diene motif to furnish stereodefined cyclohexenes and highly substituted arenes, highlighting their versatility as synthetic building blocks.

item.title: Benzylsuccinate synthase as an engineerable platform for stereoselective C–C bond formation via C–H functionalization
item.description: Stereoselective olefin hydroalkylation offers a direct route to chiral C(sp3)-rich products from simple C–H substrates, but biocatalytic platforms for this transformation are rare. Glycyl radical enzymes catalyze hydroalkylation in anaerobic metabolism, yet applications in chemical synthesis have been precluded by a lack of methods for in vitro activation. Here we use a soluble activase to unlock GRE hydroalkylases as a tunable class of radical biocatalysts. We demonstrate broad substrate scope, high stereocontrol, and preparative-scale utility, while showing through systematic mutagenesis that 17 of 18 active-site residues can be altered without loss of activity. Variants expand reactivity and alter regioselectivity. Structural analysis reveals how mutagenesis improves turnover. These results transform GRE hydroalkylases from pathway-specific metabolic enzymes into engineerable catalysts for stereocontrolled C–C bond formation.

item.title: Exploring Boltzmann Distributions via Kernel-Based Fokker–Planck Ensemble Transport
item.description: Local trajectory-based samplers can relax within a visited basin long before finite trajectories cross barriers to other Boltzmann-relevant regions. We introduce the Fokker–Planck Transformer (FPT), a training-free interacting-ensemble method that makes the instantaneous ensemble distribution a dynamical variable, shifting exploration from trajectory-wise barrier crossing toward distribution-level redistribution. FPT discretizes the current-velocity representation of overdamped Fokker–Planck evolution by combining energetic drift with a kernel estimate of the ensemble score. The continuum flow has the Boltzmann density as its stationary target and monotonically dissipates configurational free energy and relative entropy. A Gaussian row-mass selector couples increasing local occupancy to a vanishing spatial scale without a separate bandwidth limit. For its fresh explicit-Euler realization, pathwise score residuals propagate to distributional and observable errors, while a weak-flux argument gives conditional fixed-horizon convergence to the Fokker–Planck solution. For this realization, a controlled two-dimensional calculation tracks transport from a localized Gaussian toward equilibrium against a numerically propagated Fokker–Planck reference. In a three-dimensional periodic landscape, an exact Fokker–Planck reference shows that a shared-bandwidth approximation populates distant wells far ahead of the continuum solution, which accounts for its faster support discovery; the transported ensemble runs warm, and a Hastings-corrected continuation from its endpoint restores the energy distribution within two steps. Further tests in a 100-dimensional landscape, alanine decapeptide, and 190 docking systems show rapid expansion of Boltzmann-relevant support, with the clearest gains over matched local controls when barriers or configurational complexity limit global exploration. Overall, FPT provides thermodynamically grounded finite-budget support discovery and can seed target-preserving sampling.

item.title: Two-carbon annulation of primary amines to azetidines
item.description: Azetidines are valuable motifs in medicinal chemistry, yet their broader use is constrained by a lack of general, concise methods for preparing N–H azetidines from simple feedstocks. Here, we report a direct two-carbon annulation of unprotected primary alkylamines that provides α-mono- and α,α-disubstituted azetidines. Dual photoredox and hydrogen-atomtransfer catalysis enables α-C–H alkylation with vinylsulfonium reagents to generate γ-amino sulfonium intermediates, which undergo intramolecular SN2 cyclization to forge the fourmembered ring without protecting groups or prefunctionalization. Low-temperature continuous flow is critical for overriding the innate N-centered reactivity of primary amines and suppressing rapid N-alkylation by the vinylsulfonium reagent. The method uses commercially available building blocks, tolerates a range of functional groups, and provides streamlined access to azetidines that are otherwise challenging to prepare. Successful kilogram-scale translation, underpinned by process-safety assessment, demonstrates that the low-temperature flow strategy is transferable beyond discovery scale.

item.title: Design and Benchmarking of CK2α′-Preferring Inhibitors for Huntington’s Disease: The Limits of Structure-Based Isoform Selectivity
item.description: Protein kinase CK2 acts through two catalytic isoforms, CK2α (A1) and CK2α′ (A2), whose ATP-binding sites differ at only two hinge positions, making isoform-selective inhibition difficult. We tested whether a standard structure-based pipeline can design and rank CK2α′-preferring compounds. In a paired benchmark of 210 compounds measured against both isoforms, the inter-isoform docking score was unrelated to the experimental selectivity (Spearman ρ = −0.22), and even within the benzo[c][2,6]naphthyridine scaffold, the scoring reversed the order set by the ChEMBL activities. The only reliable determinant of preference, a two-carbon linker between the anilino nitrogen and the pendant ring of this scaffold, emerged from the measured activities rather than from any computed score. Molecular-dynamics ensembles of the two isoforms overlapped (0.88 Å between versus 0.72–0.96 Å within), placing the selectivity signal below the resolution of the methods. From an enumerated series, EV043 showed the largest end-point free-energy preference for CK2α′ (ΔΔGb -7.74 kcal/mol), although this value remained sensitive to the starting pose in CK2α, while the non-selective inhibitor CX-4945 was reproduced correctly (+0.08 kcal/mol). Distinguishing CK2α′ from CK2α therefore requires alchemical free-energy methods supported by experimental validation.

item.title: Limited Intrinsic CO2/CH4 Selectivity in Imine-Linked COF-LZU-1: Evidence from PBE-D3 Adsorption Energetics and Binary-Mixture Monte Carlo Simulations
item.description: Imine-linked covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are widely proposed for CO2/CH4 separation, yet the intrinsic selectivity of the archetypal framework COF-LZU1 has not been quantified against a transparent baseline. Here, periodic PBE-D3 calculations and grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations are combined to test whether pristine COF-LZU1 discriminates between CO2 and CH4. At three positions spanning the 1.8 nm channel, relaxed PBE-D3 adsorption energies are −3.10, −3.66, and −8.90 kJ mol-1 for CO2 and −3.13, −3.63, and −8.76 kJ mol-1 for CH4; CO2 binds more strongly than CH4 by at most 0.14 kJ mol-1, at the confined site near the imine linkage. Consistently, GCMC simulations of equimolar mixtures (TraPPE, DREIDING, DDEC6 charges, Ewald electrostatics, 14 Å cutoff with analytic tail corrections) give low selectivities of 1.15–1.71 between 273 and 323 K and 0.1–10 bar, and 1.20–1.38 at 298 K, rising with pressure and falling with temperature. At 223 K and 7–10 bar, CO2 fills about 80% of the pore volume and the selectivity reaches about 11, a pore-filling effect and not intrinsic discrimination. Replacing EPM2 CO2, a 12 Å cutoff, and no tail corrections by the final force-field set raises the selectivity by 7–27%, so selectivities near unity are force-field sensitive. The weak simulated selectivity, together with the near-equal DFT binding energies, defines a baseline that functionalization, for example with Ag+, must overcome.

item.title: FOdorant conformational ensembles encode topology, molecular size and polar-surface coherence, not shape
item.description: Odor is widely modelled as three-dimensional shape recognition: a flexible odorant presents a 300 K conformer ensemble to a receptor repertoire, implying that perceptual breadth peaks at an intermediate number of accessible shapes and that explicit 3D representations outperform 2D molecular graphs. We test both predictions under a cryptographically pre-registered plan across catalogue profiles (n = 4,808), human psychophysics (n = 304) and heterologous receptor arrays (n = 294). Computing 300 K GFN2-xTB ensembles at a 200-conformer ceiling for all 1,821 flexible cohort members (106,526 conformers) and benchmarking 21 neural representations across 10 seeds, we find that neither claim holds. Conformational entropy saturates by 28 conformers (88% attained at a ceiling of 20), excluding an interior breadth optimum sixfold below the populated range (β2 = +0.0080, 95% CI -0.0014 to +0.0172). No 3D representation outperforms a capacity-matched or descriptor-augmented 2D graph. Out-of-sample-replicated confound analyses show that 3D shape dispersion vanishes once chain topology is controlled; instead, breadth reflects coarse topological flexibility (peaking at 9.2 rotatable bonds), molecular extent and polar-surface coherence (concave β2 = -0.0264). Keywords: conformational ensemble · odor breadth · molecular representation · Artificial Intelligence · Graph Neural Network

item.title: Analytic Electrostatic Embedding of MACE-POLAR for Fixed-Charge ML/MM
item.description: Electrostatic embedding allows a local machine-learning potential to respond to an extended molecular environment without including every environmental atom in its message-passing graph. We construct a fixed-charge machine-learning/molecular-mechanics (ML/MM) interface for the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model. Analytic Gaussian monopole and dipole operators supply the environmental potential, the internal electrostatic features, and the interaction energy. Differentiation through both field-conditioned density updates gives forces on the model fragment and the environment, which are combined with a subtractive classical energy and exact link-atom force redistribution. A reciprocal-space extension treats three-dimensional periodicity at fixed cell. We assess the implementation using fixed-geometry numerical checks and 24 matched QM/MM reference calculations for a 2589-atom rhodopsin model, with 54 atoms in the neural-network graph. The analytic model gives a relative-energy root-mean-square error of 8.62 kJ mol−1 after one constant energy shift, and force-component errors of 0.07345 and 0.00797 eV Å−1 on the 53 real high-level atoms and 2536 environmental atoms, respectively. Analytic operators substantially reduce rotational errors while leaving the QM/MM accuracy essentially unchanged. A nearby water accounts for approximately 74% of the environmental squared force error. Matched charge-density and frozen-density force comparisons identify limitations of both the local multipole representation and its predicted coefficients. The results establish the numerical consistency of the embedding implementation and delimit the single-point accuracy of the transferred pretrained model.

item.title: Pairwise learning of cyclic peptide membrane permeability on a matched-molecular-pair graph
item.description: Cyclic peptides are a promising drug scaffold that can target proteins considered undruggable by small molecules, but their poor membrane permeability limits further application. Deep learning has been used to lower the wet-lab burden of finding cell-permeable peptides. Most existing models are trained on measurements curated from many publications and predict a single peptide’s permeability directly. That formulation ignores systematic measurement differences between publications, and it does not answer the actual question drug development asks: not whether a peptide is permeable, but which modification would make a given lead peptide more permeable. Here we introduce CycPeptMMP, which learns the permeability difference within a matched molecular pair (denoted as pair mode) instead of a single peptide’s value (denoted as single mode). Conventional molecular pairing approaches do not apply to cyclic peptides, so we constructed a graph of matched molecular pairs over the four modification types commonly used to improve permeability, organizing 5,674 peptides across seven publication sources. We trained both single and pair modes on five graph neural network backbones across 10 random splits. Pair mode performs better on sources with fewer than 1,000 peptides except Wang, whose peptides often lack a close analogue. Pair mode’s advantage is greatest for the closest analogues differing by a single modification. Single mode is preferable for sources with more than 1,000 peptides. We also implemented a censored loss to retain peptides with clamped measurements in the regression. For pairs involving those peptides, pair mode is more accurate when predicting which one in the pair is more permeable. Taken together, we provide a framework for comparing single and pair mode within each source, and show where pair mode is worth using.

item.title: Quantifying trends across a series of leaving groups in mixtures containing ionic liquids
item.description: The nucleofugality of fluoride was measured in a range of solvent mixtures containing ionic liquids. The first order rate constants associated with the solvolysis of the fluorides of well-described electrofuges were determined in mixtures of ethanol and different proportions of the ionic liquid 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide. Temperature-dependent kinetic analyses allowed determination of activation parameters and rationalisation of observed solvent effects in different ionic liquid mixtures through consideration of solvent interactions with species along the reaction coordinate. From the solvolysis data of those fluorides, the nucleofugality of fluoride was determined in these systems. Further, the nucleofugality of fluoride was determined in mixtures containing high proportions of six additional ionic liquids in ethanol. These data allowed for quantification of the effects of varying both the amount of ionic liquid present in the reaction mixture, as well as the component ions, on the nucleofugality of fluoride. Importantly, several differences were noted in both the microscopic origin of the solvent effects and hence the nature of the effects of different ionic liquids on the nucleofugality of fluoride in comparison to previously studied halogen leaving groups, highlighting the importance of nucleofuge size and charge density in understanding the origins of the observed reactivities.

item.title: UEFCCS: A Multimodal Deep Learning Framework with Fine-Tuned 3D Molecular Representations for Collision Cross Section Prediction
item.description: Collision cross section (CCS), derived from ion mobility spectrometry, provides a valuable reference for analyte identification. Achieving high predictive accuracy and effective extrapolation to structurally dissimilar molecules, however, remains challenging for existing machine-learning models. Here, we present UEFCCS, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates molecular formula encoding and fingerprints with CCS-adapted three-dimensional (3D) molecular representations, obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained Transformer encoder using only [M+H]+ CCS data from the training set. item.title: Halochromic response of a prickly pear fruit (Opuntia ficus-indica) extract in solution and in gelatin films: an exploratory study
item.description: Smart packaging uses natural pigments that change color depending on pH. An extract was obtained from prickly pears of Opuntia ficus-indica using MeOH:H2O 1:4, and its visible spectrum (400–700 nm) was evaluated in Britton–Robinson buffer solutions with nominal pH values ranging from 2 to 12. In the visible spectrum, absorption bands were observed at 534-536 nm, with stable absorbance (A535 = 0.257-0.259) between pH 4 and 7, a bathochromic shift to 542-548 nm accompanied by a decrease in intensity at pH 9-11, and an almost complete loss of the band at pH 12. This behavior is consistent with that of betacyanins. The neutral extract was incorporated into glycerol-plasticized gelatin films, which exhibited the amide A, I, II, and III bands of the matrix in their ATR-FTIR spectra, with no bands attributable to the pigment. The films changed from pink to yellow upon exposure to 0.1 M KOH and NH3 vapors, producing changes in the IR spectra mainly within the 1650–1400 cm−1 region. This exploratory study lays the groundwork for using the extract in a gelatin matrix as an intelligent packaging material for shrimp, whose degradation produces biogenic amines that alkalinize the surrounding environment.

item.title: Light-Induced Synthesis of Ultra Thick Polymer Brush Coatings with Boosted Antifogging Properties
item.description: Polymer brushes with thicknesses exceeding 500 nm are synthetically challenging and rarely reported, while their applications remain largely unexplored. A range of applications, including catalytic, antifriction, and antifogging/antifreezing surfaces, could greatly benefit from their highly packed and extended conformation. Very recently, ultra-thick (200–3000 nm) polymer brushes have been demonstrated with largely improved wear bearing in antifriction tests. Herein, we demonstrate eosin Y-mediated SI-PhotoATRP to generate poly(oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether)methacrylate (POEGMEMA) brushes up to 800 nm thick, easily tunable with green-light intensity. The series of polymer brushes ranging from 30 to 800 nm were systematically tested against fogging under cooling. The developed testing setup enabled detection of dew points, whose 2 shifts were most significant for the thickest POEGMEMA brushes, with a striking shift of 9 °C at 0.5 °Cmin−1. The analysis at different cooling rates enabled the decoupling of kinetic and thermodynamic components of the antifogging of polymer brushes for the first time. Our work exemplifies a synthetic route toward generation of ultra-thick polymer brushes and strongly supports their need for further structure-property relationship studies and potential applications.

item.title: Zincrius-8: An Automated Multi-Position Flow Reactor for the On-Demand Generation of Organozinc Reagents and Their Direct Use in Negishi Coupling
item.description: Among common carbon nucleophiles, organozinc reagents are notable for tolerating esters, nitriles, Bocprotected amines, and other sensitive groups in C-C bond-formation reactions. However, few are sold commercially, and their solutions degrade on storage. Herein, we report Zincrius-8, an automated flow reactor that converts a packed bed of commercial granular zinc into an on-demand source of organozinc solutions. Using a unified protocol that does not require LiCl or other additives, primary and secondary alkyl iodides afford the corresponding reagents in DMA in over 90% yield. The same protocol also provides tertiary, Reformatsky, allyl, and propargyl reagents, though in lower yields. In 151 runs with 44 organic halides, the reactor delivered titrated solutions on a scale of up to 1.2 mol per run. These solutions go directly into the next step: in a screen of 192 Negishi couplings, the product was formed in 43 of 48 aryl halide/organozinc combinations, and two couplings were repeated on a gram scale. Bed lifespan is limited by the build-up of fines and changes to the zinc surface, rather than by zinc consumption, so it is simply replaced after five cycles. Organozinc reagents thus become on-demand reagents rather than stock positions.

item.title: Feedback-regulation between imination reactions and coacervation
item.description: Herein, we investigate the feedback-regulation between imination reactions and coacervate phase formation. Partial imination of long-chain polylysine rapidly generates micrometre-sized coacervate droplets, whereas the corresponding reaction with a monomeric lysine model remains strongly disfavored. Subtle changes in the structure and charge distribution of anionic aldehydes determine whether the reaction produces soluble species, liquid coacervates or solid-like aggregates. Remarkably, the formation of the condensed phase produces a ca. 60-fold enhancement in the apparent imination equilibrium constant, revealing strong thermodynamic coupling between dynamic covalent bond formation and coacervation. Polymer-length dependence further establishes the importance of multivalency, while non-reactive substrate analogues and dynamic covalent scavenging experiments demonstrate that imine formation is required to trigger phase-separation. Finally, we show that this coupling can operate within multicomponent dynamic covalent libraries, where coacervation biases chemical selection towards the phase-forming constituent and competing species can strongly modulate condensate stability. Together, these results establish dynamic covalent charge editing as a strategy for generating adaptive peptide-based coacervates in which chemical composition and phase behaviour reciprocally regulate one another

item.title: Accelerating Adsorption-Site Screening on Forsterite with Foundation Potentials
item.description: The binding energies (BEs) of molecules on ice-free silicate grains determine their release in the inner regions of protoplanetary discs, but their distributions over adsorption sites are too costly to obtain with density functional theory (DFT) alone. Here, we assess eight foundation potentials as released, i.e. without further training, against dispersion-corrected DFT (PBE-D3) for the screening of adsorption sites on forsterite (Mg2SiO4) surfaces, and find that their errors on reference BEs, of 6.7 kJ mol−1 or more, are in large part an offset for each molecule. Of the two potentials screened, MACE-MH-1 locates the strongest adsorption states as often as a potential fine-tuned on the mineral: in one screening of four molecules on three facets, its minima contain the strongest known PBE-D3 state in 10–11 of 12 pairs, against 10 for the latter, whose minima yielded most of these states. Its BEs, however, require PBE-D3 refinement, since its strongest minimum is underbound by 5.0 kJ mol−1 on average, and on (111) no single screening returns every strongest state, which a DFT check recovers. On (010), the strongest Mg-bound states bind five molecules 2.6–4.5 times more strongly than amorphous water ice, suggesting that bare silicate grains retain them to higher temperatures.

item.title: CARBONYLATION AS A STRATEGIC TOOL: Pd-CATALYZED ACCESS TO (HETERO)ARYLACETIC ACID DERIVATIVES FROM BENZYL-TYPE HALIDES
item.description: Carbonylation of benzyl-type halides offers a one-step route to otherwise difficult-to-access (hetero)arylacetic acid derivatives, but competing reactions and substrate-dependent reactivity substantially limit the applicability of this approach. In this work, we examined possible outcomes across a broad preparative series using a Pd-dppf catalyst system, with multiple examples exceeding 100 g. The study reports successful ester formation alongside methyl ether formation, incomplete conversion, and decomposition across diverse heterocyclic frameworks. Isolation and crystallographic characterization of [Pd(dppf)(CO)2] motivated a study of CO pressure. Lowering the initial pressure from 20 to 5 atm increased isolated ester yields by 28-66 % in six preparative comparisons. This response is consistent with inhibition by excess CO, although the abundance and kinetic role of the isolated complex during turnover remain unresolved. Importantly, pressure adjustment did not eliminate competing substitution for all substrates. In particular, 2,6-dimethylbenzyl chloride and bromide exhibited markedly different ester/ether distributions at the same pressure and temperature. These results distinguish low-yielding preparations that respond to changes in conditions from cases in which substitution or decomposition persists. They provide practical starting points for extending benzyl-type carbonylation while defining the limits of structural generalizations from substrate-scope data.

item.title: OPRD-target: A Collection of Manufacturing Chemistry Targets for Benchmarking Retrosynthesis Tools
item.description: Modern computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) tools, particularly retrosynthesis planning, are becoming practical aids for the ideation stage of chemical synthesis design. However, the same target molecule can be synthesized via substantially different routes depending on the purpose: a discovery or medicinal chemistry route used to obtain small quantities during early development, or a manufactur-ing route optimized for industrial-scale production. While CASP tools have been extensively studied and benchmarked for the former, their ability to support manufacturing route design remains largely unexplored. Performance of CASP tools is usually measured by benchmark experiments, which typi-cally report the fraction of target molecules for which a tool can generate a synthesis route, connecting the target molecule through a sequence of intermediates to starting materials. Sometimes, to assess the quality of the generated routes, they are also manually compared with expert-designed routes reported in the literature. Currently, public benchmark datasets focused on process and manufacturing chemistry are lacking. To address this gap, we take a first step toward developing a benchmark for evaluating CASP tools in manufacturing chemistry by systematically analyzing publications in Organic Process Research & Development (OPRD). We reviewed OPRD papers published between 1997 and 2022 and selected 1915 papers reporting multi-step synthesis routes. We then separately collected and digitized the target molecules of corresponding synthesis routes as SMILES strings. This resulted in a collection of 2219 unique target molecules, each paired with the DOI of the original publication reporting their corresponding synthesis route. This benchmark can therefore be used to assess how many process-chemistry targets modern CASP tools can solve and, for solved targets, to compare predicted routes with the expert-designed ones reported in the literature. The dataset is publicly available at: https://github.com/KagakuLab/OPRD-target.

item.title: How Multiconfigurational Is Zeaxanthin? A Natural Orbital Functional Study of Its Ground and Excited States
item.description: The electronic structure of zeaxanthin presents an important challenge for understanding the relationship between electron correlation, multiconfigurational character, and optical excitations in conjugated systems. In this work, we investigate its ground and excited states using natural orbital functional (NOF) theory combined with the extended random phase approximation (ERPA). Our results reveal that the apparent multiconfigurational character of the ground state depends strongly on the treatment of electron correlation. PNOF7, which incorporates static but not dynamic interpair correlation, predicts a more pronounced multiconfigurational character, consistent with the picture emerging from other multireference approaches. In contrast, the modified global NOF (GNOFm), which incorporates both static and dynamic interpair correlation, yields occupations closer to their integer limits. The excited state calculations reveal a weak low energy excitation followed by a strongly allowed transition, consistent with the characteristic dark and bright states of conjugated polyenes. The weak excitation exhibits a pronounced sensitivity to the extent of the correlated orbital space, whereas the intense transition depends more strongly on the ERPA approximation. Analysis of the response vectors further reveals distinct electronic characteristics, with a broadly distributed response for the weak state and a more concentrated response for the intense transition. These findings demonstrate that the interpretation of multiconfigurational character and electronic excitations in conjugated systems depends critically on a balanced treatment of static and dynamic electron correlation.

item.title: Buffer Ionization as the Dominant Source of Redox Entropy in Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer
item.description: Proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) underpins a wide range of energy conversion technologies, from artificial photosynthesis to electrocatalytic fuel production. In thermoelectrochemical cells (thermocells), PCET-active transition metal complexes can give large temperature coefficients (α) by leveraging the substantial entropy changes associated with simultaneous electron and proton transfers. However, the fundamental origin of this entropy change and how it is modulated by the electrolyte environment remain elusive. Here we report a soluble ruthenium biimidazole complex, [Ru(hexylbiim)3](PF6)2 (hexylbiim = 1-hexyl-2,2′-biimidazole), in which the N-hexyl groups overcome the poor solubility of the parent [Ru(biim)3]2+ and allow its PCET to be studied over a wide pH range. This Ru complex has three dissociable protons, and the three pKa values of each of the RuII and RuIII states are obtained from variable-pH UV-vis spectroscopy and square-wave voltammetry. Between pH 6.5 and 8.1, RuII releases three protons upon oxidation, and |α| reaches its maximum, α = −3.76 mV K−1, which corresponds to a reaction entropy (ΔSrc) of −363 J K−1 mol−1. The pH dependence of α matches the theoretical curve calculated from the number of transferred protons and the ionization entropy of the buffer species. This result shows that the redox entropy of the PCET couple is largely supplied by the buffer, and that the buffer is therefore as important as the redox molecule in the design of PCET-based thermocells.

item.title: Virtual Intact Block Extraction: Reconstruction of Molecular Assemblies across Periodic Boundaries
item.description: Reconstructing molecular assemblies across periodic boundaries requires accurate periodic placement in general triclinic cells and a criterion for whether a stored frame uniquely defines a finite assembly. Existing tools return one arrangement per frame without indicating whether contacts fix it, and voxel-based or multistep workflows can split contacting subunits in tilted cells or depend on coordinate origin and cell basis. Here, Virtual Intact Block Extraction (VIBE) is introduced to combine exact closest-lattice-point placement of topology-defined parts with an algebraic analysis of the periodic contact graph. A frame uniquely determines the relative placement of its parts when this graph is connected and every cycle sums to zero; a nonzero cycle identifies a boundary-spanning assembly such as a filament or membrane. Every designed synthetic assembly was recovered; in biomolecular trajectories, peptide contacts broken by voxel bridging were preserved, and outputs did not change with coordinate origin or cell basis.

item.title: Rate Theory of Modulated Steps: Mass Action and Fractional Orders from Thermal and Strong Coupling
item.description: Transition-state theory describes an elementary step in which one complex changes. In many catalytic steps, a second complex, the modulator, such as a proton, an electron or an ion, is bound on one side only. We derive the rate law of this modulated step in chemical potentials. If the modulator moves like the atoms of the complex (thermal coupling), its amount enters by mass action. If it binds and releases faster than the complex changes (strong coupling), its amount acts as an energy, with fractional orders. Electrocatalysis treats the electron in this way. Fractional pH orders are reported throughout electrochemistry, each with its own explanation. The exchange rate separates the two cases, which the speed of the modulator selects. On platinum, the exchange rate of hydrogen underpotential deposition changes little over alkaline pH. This excludes mass action of the hydroxide ion and agrees with strong coupling or an intermediate modulation speed. Strong coupling gives a Butler–Volmer law with pH.

item.title: Programming Polymer Lifecycle through Catalyst-Free Photodepolymerization and Value-Added Upcycling
item.description: The durability and functional versatility of polymeric materials underpin their widespread use, yet also contribute to persistent plastic waste and the formation of micro/nanoplastics throughout the polymer lifecycle. Developing polymer systems that reconcile functional performance with controlled depolymerization and value-added upcycling remains a major challenge. Here, we demonstrated a functional polymer platform with intrinsic photooxidative cleavage by repurposing conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds as programmed cleavage sites within polymer backbones. The resulting polyamides and polyurethane undergo catalystfree depolymerization under ambient conditions, incorporating oxygen from air to yield structurally defined carbonyl-containing products. Contrary to the conventional paradigm, aggregation accelerates depolymerization by reshaping excited-state dynamics and promoting ROS generation, revealing an unexpected role of aggregation in driving photochemical depolymerization. Concurrently, the evolution of fluorescence provides an intrinsic optical readout of the depolymerization process. Notably, this strategy enables the photochemical transformation of micro/nanoplastic-like particles in water under natural sunlight, extending the cleavage pathway beyond bulk materials. Importantly, the resulting photoproducts resist further oxidation while retaining distinct photophysical and photoactivated properties, realizing value-added utilization. By coupling polymer functionality, programmed photodepolymerization, and product valorization, this work establishes a versatile design principle for controlling polymer lifecycles and advancing sustainable functional materials.

item.title: Ionic routers encode GPCR activation state on both sides of the membrane
item.description: In both class A and B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), certain charged residues exchange one salt-bridge partner for another between the active and inactive states: each binds one oppositely charged residue in the active state and a different one in the inactive state, with neither partner bound in both. Their ionic bonds are rerouted rather than lost, and neither state leaves them free. Such residues are called ionic routers [1]. We report the complete set of ionic routers the structural record deposited in the Protein Data Bank supports across class A and B1 receptors, and the first evidence in any GPCR that the arrangement reaches the extracellular face. Our earlier screen fixed the 4.0 angstrom salt-bridge cutoff in advance [1]. Here the screen is given only the pattern of contacts a router must show, and the cutoff is solved for. Enumerating every charged three-residue arrangement that 762 deposited structures of the 61 class A and B1 receptors with structures in both activation states can evaluate reduces 7,266 directed triples to 211 in which a pivot is opposed in charge by both partners. Two meet the definition, both required bonds placed above majority occupancy by a 95 percent interval: on activation, rhodopsin E247 (6.30x30) exchanges R135 (3.50x50) for K231 (5.66x66), releasing the contact the ionic lock literature describes, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) E408 (8.49x49) exchanges R348 (6.37x37) for R176 (2.46x46). These are the two reported previously, recovered here without that criterion: a test of the earlier ranking measure, not a repetition of it. The two-router answer holds across a contiguous window from 3.75 to 4.25 angstroms, with the conventional 4.0 interior to it. Below the window only rhodopsin survives. Each router sits on the most deeply sampled receptor in its class, rhodopsin of 56 in class A and GLP-1R of 5 in class B1. Only 13 of 61 receptors carry four or more scorable structures on any arrangement’s weaker arm, the minimum at which selection is possible. Router discovery is record-limited.

item.title: Chemical Filtering of Thymine over Uracil by Differential Hydrolysis under Dark Alkaline Hydrothermal-Vent Conditions: A Mass-Consistent, Control-Restrained Simulation Framework (UPDSF v6.7.0)
item.description: A central question in prebiotic chemistry is why modern DNA contains thymine (5-methyluracil) rather than uracil. Most proposed answers invoke surface UV photochemistry, yet alkaline hydrothermal vents—a leading candidate cradle for prebiotic synthesis—are dark environments. Here we present UPDSF v6.7.0, a mass-consistent, kinetically-consistent, provenance-tracked simulation framework that tests whether differential hydrolysis stability alone can chemically filter thymine over uracil in dark, alkaline, high-temperature conditions. At the model optimum (90 °C, in-situ pH 11, 240 h, zero photon flux), differential hydrolysis with an Arrhenius-extrapolated rate ratio k_U/k_T ≈ 357 raises the DNA T/(U+T) fraction from below the feedstock level under a no-selection control (0.67× influx, i.e. net T depletion) to 2.02× influx in the baseline—a controlcorrected enrichment of ≈ 3.0× that is immune to the assumed influx stoichiometry and to the CSI normalization convention, because both arms of the decisive sweep share every assumption. A preregistered decisive control sweep (7 arms × 20 seeds) refutes any single-channel explanation: suppressing the polymer-side or the free-monomer-side hydrolysis differential alone collapses part of the enrichment (CSI 3.47 → 2.83 and 2.46 respectively), while suppressing both eliminates it (CSI 1.80)—chemical T-over-U filtering acts at both the monomer and polymer levels, with the 2 free-monomer channel dominant under the assumed free-hydrolysis scale. An opt-in sequenceresolved Darwinian layer (100-residue copolymers, Wright–Fisher reproduction, templatedependent misincorporation) shows that replication amplifies the chemistry-built T-skew with a control-corrected gain of only ≈ 1.06×; without mutation the population freezes as a clone at 0.39 pop T/(U+T), and without replication the population goes extinct in 10/10 seeds. The reported optimum is a horizon-edge value: enrichment is still rising at 240 h (3.46×) and continues to 10.2× at 10,000 h while survival decays to 0.32; we therefore report the control-corrected metric, not the absolute CSI, as the headline. All 110 parameters carry explicit provenance (47 literature, 44 assumed, 15 imposed, 3 derived, 1 extrapolated), and the framework closes mass balance to a maximum relative error of 5.7 × 10-15 across a 572-cell sensitivity grid with exactly zero consumedidentity residuals.

item.title: Optimization and Microstructural Analysis of Underwater Friction Stir Welding of AA6063 Aluminum Alloy
item.description: Currently, there is a significant demand for lightweight materials, such as aluminum (Al) alloys, in the aviation, aerospace, marine, and automotive sectors. However, manufacturing industries face significant challenges in producing a defect-free joint between these metals. Al alloys are used extensively in the manufacturing sector to meet the varying demands of customers and traders. This is primarily due to exceptional characteristics such as reduced weight, corrosion resistance, and improved mechanical properties. It offers unique performance in terms of low density, high strength, ease of processing, cost-effectiveness, etc., setting it apart from conventional production materials. This study experimentally investigates the control of the productivity and quality of the friction stir welding (FSW) process using response surface methodology (RSM), specifically the Box-Behnken Design (BBD). In the present work, Al6063 plates are welded using D2 steel tool shoulders and HSS tool pins. The optimal ultimate tensile strength (UTS-134.625 MPa) was determined by analyzing three parameters: rotating tool speed, tool traverse speed, and pin length. It was found that excessive material flow entering the plate primarily produced voids, resulting in defect-free welding. It has superior mechanical strength and a fine surface, as validated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) findings. This proposed approach could benefit the manufacturing sector by enabling the formation of sound welds of alloys for heavy assembly applications.

item.title: Desolvation-Based Encapsulation of Nanoparticles in Protein Nanocarriers: From Multilabel Nanocomposites to Biosensing Reagents
item.description: Effective surface functionalization is a key requirement for the application of nanoparticles in biomedicine. Protein-based coatings offer a versatile solution, providing abundant functional groups, colloidal stabilization, and a well-established basis for bioconjugation. This review examines desolvation as a method for encapsulating nanoparticles within covalently cross-linked protein matrices, yielding nanocomposites that can contain multiple nanoparticles within a single protein carrier. Although desolvation is widely used to prepare drug-loaded nanocarriers, this review considers it from a different perspective, focusing on its potential for preparing nanocomposites for biosensing. Analysis of the literature demonstrates that desolvation is a versatile approach capable of encapsulating nanoparticles of different sizes, structures, and surface chemistries. It enables the preparation of nanocomposite labels with unique combinations of properties for prospective analytical applications, including surface-enhanced Raman scattering, magnetic, fluorescence, Förster resonance energy transfer, catalytic, and stimulus-responsive systems. Desolvation-derived nanocomposites can exhibit good short- and long-term stability and can be produced at tens-of-grams scale under laboratory conditions. Potential sources of irreproducibility in desolvation and non-specific interactions arising from the cross-linked protein matrix are also discussed. By linking the synthesis of protein–nanoparticle composites to the requirements of diagnostic assays, this review outlines how desolvation-based nanocomposites may serve as practical multilabel reagents for established and emerging bioanalytical formats.

item.title: Subspace Fokker–Planck Transformer: An Ensemble-Based Framework for Accelerated Free-Energy Sampling
item.description: Rare transitions between metastable states limit the convergence of molecular free-energy calculations. Here, we introduce the subspace Fokker–Planck Transformer (sFPT), an ensemble-based enhancedsampling method that transports the instantaneous replica distribution in a selected collective-variable (CV) subspace. sFPT estimates the score of the evolving CV distribution using a kernel representation of the replica ensemble, maps the resulting entropy force to atomic coordinates through the CV Jacobian, and incorporates this force into underdamped Langevin dynamics.
