We show that the self-consistent stationary CV distribution satisfies PCV ∞ (s) ∝ [PCV phys(s)] λ/(1+λ), yielding a controllably flattened free-energy surface, and establish convergence of the ideal mean-field dynamics through a nonincreasing Lyapunov functional. Post-convergence trajectories can be accumulated to improve the statistical precision of freeenergy reconstruction. We evaluate sFPT on alanine dipeptide in vacuum and explicit water, alanine tetrapeptide in a three-dimensional CV space, and a Claisen rearrangement described by an ML/MM potential in explicit water. The reconstructed free-energy landscapes agree with umbrella-sampling, replica-exchange, and well-tempered metadynamics (WT-MetaD) references. For alanine dipeptide in vacuum and explicit water, comparisons at matched walker numbers show that both methods can benefit from parallel sampling. For the Claisen rearrangement, sFPT reaches sustained agreement with the reference basin free-energy difference after approximately 24 ps per replica, whereas the selected 64-walker WT-MetaD calculation retains slow deviations over 400 ps per walker. This advantage remains visible when the integration steps over all replicas are counted. These results establish instantaneous ensemble transport as a practical route to stable free-energy estimates from many short parallel trajectories.

item.title: Finite-Depth Response Selection of Higher Excitations in Correlated Wave-Function Methods
item.description: We introduce finite-depth response selection (FDRS), a non-iterative finite-depth framework for constructing higher-excitation spaces, with a universal formulation across wave-function ansätz and excitation ranks. Starting from a converged lower-rank solution, FDRS propagates the preconditioned response of the omitted space for a prescribed depth and constructs the retained higher-excitation space in a single selection step, without iterative reselection. To test the generality of this construction, we apply FDRS without method-specific modification to two qualitatively different projected wave-function problems: variational CI and nonlinear CC. In CISD→FCI benchmarks, FDRS recovers near-millihartree accuracy with variational spaces of only 104–105 determinants, including through the strongly correlated region of HF bond dissociation. When transferred unchanged to CCSD→CCSDTQ, FDRS reduces the energy error below 0.1mEh for all six small molecules while retaining only 5–15% of the complete T3 ⊕ T4 manifolds. These results demonstrate that finite-depth response provides a compact, transferable criterion for identifying important higher excitations across distinct wave-function parametrizations.

item.title: High Li+ Transference Number of a Novel Fluorine-Free Lithium Salt in Carbonate Electrolyte: DFT and Molecular Dynamics Insights into Dilithium 2,5-Dioxopiperazine-1,4-Disulfonate (LiDPSO)
item.description: Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly constrained by the drawbacks of fluorinecontaining commercial lithium salts, including hydrolysis hazards and the environmental burden of fluorinated species. Developing fluorine-free lithium salts with a high Li+ transference number tLi may offer a route to avoid fluoride-derived hazards, mitigate concentration polarization, and potentially lower lithium dendrite risks in applicable cell systems. Inspired by the zwitterion shielding effect, this work proposes an intramolecular likecharge shielding (ILCS) conceptual model and computationally examines a novel fluorine-free salt, dilithium 2,5-dioxopiperazine-1,4-disulfonate (LiDPSO), in EC/DMC carbonate electrolytes using density functional theory (DFT) and large-scale all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. DFT cluster–continuum and nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations reveal that the covalently anchored dual sulfonate sites provide intramolecular like-charge shielding that facilitates dissociation of the first Li+, whereas dissociation of the second Li+ is energetically unfavorable, favoring the contact ion pair [LiA]-. Continued solvation of [LiA]- enlarges its hydrodynamic radius and suppresses anion diffusion, which is expected to raise tLi. Backbone carbonyl groups build an intramolecular solvation microenvironment, enabling low-barrier Li+ hopping between the two sulfonate sites in [LiA]-. In MD simulations (>105 atoms systems), benefiting from combined vehicular transport, intramolecular hopping and Grotthuss-like Li+ exchange, the system achieves a high simulated tLi of ~0.73–0.74, versus ~0.41 for LiPF6, while retaining a Li+ conductivity comparable to that of LiPF6. Absolute simulated values may deviate from experiment, yet relative trends are often reproducible. If future experiments confirm both a high tLi and an acceptable Li+ conductivity for LiDPSO, this compound would be a promising fluorine-free lithium salt candidate, and the ILCS conceptual model, associated intramolecular coordination and symmetric dual-site motifs could offer new design guidelines for other innovative lithium salt anions.

item.title: Fluorination-Enabled Stereochemical Editing of Sialic Acid
item.description: Sialic acids trace the evolutionary arc of contemporary glycoscience and continue to provide inspiration for drug discovery. However, harnessing the potential of sialic acids in a therapeutic context is contingent on unlocking chemical space and devising strategies that allow the venerable C9 framework to be selectively modified in an operationally simple manner. Enabled by judicious C(sp3)-F installation at C3, the configuration of this center can serve as a lever to facilitate a series of structural editing events in a programmable fashion. This is exemplified by the regiodiversity of amide cyclization: (R)-configuration → 5-membered ring formation; (S)configuration → 7-membered ring formation with concomitant acetyl migration, to access bridged-bicyclic scaffolds that are reminiscent of naturally occurring sialic acids. Importantly, this [CH2 → CHF] isosteric replacement enables selective modification at C2 (glycosylation), C4 (epimerization) and C5 (N-deacetylation). Given the ubiquity of C3 fluorinated sialic acids in chemical biology and biomedicine, it is envisaged that this conceptual framework will expedite chemical space exploration.

item.title: Incorporating Dynamic Correlation into Grouped-Bath Configuration Interaction with Pair-Density Functional Theory
item.description: We incorporate dynamic correlation into grouped-bath configuration interaction (GBCI) using pair-density functional theory (PDFT). Computing the on-top pair density of GBCI with the conventional cumulant-based scheme requires substantial computational time and memory. We overcome this bottleneck by computing the on-top pair density directly using exact factorization. We assess state-specific GB-PDFT and its short-range variant, GB-srPDFT, together with multistate GB-PDFT variants employing the extended-multistate (XMS) and linearized (L) formulations and fragment-charge-difference (FCD) diabatization. Both PDFT and srPDFT improve vertical excitation energies. XMS-and FCD-GB-PDFT improve the description of the avoided crossing of LiF. Among the multistate schemes, FCD-GB-PDFT shows the weakest dependence on the number of interacting states. These results suggest that FCD-GB-PDFT is a promising candidate for future GBCI-based nonadiabatic dynamics simulations.

item.title: AIMETRY: GEOMETRY-SENSITIVE 3D MOLECULAR REPRESENTATIONS FROM QUANTUM MECHANICAL LEARNED FEATURES
item.description: Quantifying molecular similarity depends on both chemical composition and 3D structure, which are difficult to capture in a single fixed-length representation. Contrastive learning is a common machine learning approach to generate such representations (molecular embeddings), pulling each molecule toward a positive anchor of itself. These anchors typically come from graph augmentations that alter chemical identity or from other conformers of the same molecule. However, using conformers as positive anchors in standard contrastive learning suppresses geometric distinctions and graded structural relationships. Here, we introduce AIMetry, a geometry-sensitive representation learning scheme in which a graph transformer aggregates spatially and chemically aware atomic features from AIMNet2, a machine-learned interatomic potential trained on quantum-chemical data, into a molecular embedding. We guide standard contrastive learning using fingerprint similarity, which modulates embedding similarity between different-molecule pairs, and root-mean-square deviation, which modulates embedding similarity between conformer pairs. Trained on approximately 44 million conformers of 2.8 million ChEMBL molecules, AIMetry demonstrates higher retention of fingerprint-defined structural relationships and greater geometric sensitivity than a reference model pretrained with standard contrastive learning. AIMetry also improves linear-probe performance relative to the reference model across the evaluated datasets, while benefits under nonlinear readout and fine-tuning are task-specific. Chemical and conformational analyses provide complementary evidence about the information retained in the representation.

item.title: N-Alkyl Cyanopyridinium Salts as Modular N-Terminal Cysteine Warheads for Site-Specific Bioconjugation and Living Cell Engineering
item.description: Site-specific protein modification is central to chemical biology and to therapeutic development. Stringent control over a single site delivers homogeneous conjugates and underpins the synthetic engineering of proteins and cells, which demands streamlined and reliable chemistry. An N-terminal cysteine (NCys) represents a unique canonical amino acid handle easily incorporated into peptides, proteins, and cells, yet its use remains underexplored. Building on 2-cyanobenzothiazole (CBT), we show that quaternizing the ring nitrogen of an otherwise sluggish cyanopyridine gives N-alkyl 4-cyanopyridinium salts (4CP+) with markedly improved kinetics, aqueous solubility, synthetic accessibility, and modularity. Moreover, 4CP+ reacts selectively with NCys to deliver a wide range of biochemical reporters and tumor-receptor ligands to peptides and proteins, enabling modular assembly of functional conjugates, as exemplified by smallmolecule–protein hybrid T cell engagers. We further developed a divinyl 4CP+ that rebridges native disulfides while retaining the nitrile as a latent handle for late-stage payload installation, extending NCys chemistry to modular synthesis of homogeneous therapeutic conjugates from cyclic peptides to off-theshelf monoclonal antibodies. We also demonstrated that a genetically encoded NCys serves as a minimal conjugation tag, which, paired with 4CP+ reagents, achieves site-specific protein labeling on live cell surfaces, including a natural killer cell line, opening up cell-conjugation applications.

item.title: Fabrication of a Bimetallic NiFe-Prussian Blue-MoS2 Nano-heterojunction for NIR-Triggered Antibacterial Activity
item.description: Bacterial infections continue to pose a major threat to human health globally, and the rapid emergence of antibiotic-resistant microorganisms has created an urgent need for development of effective non-antibiotic therapeutic strategies for pathogen eradication. In this work, a series of peroxidase-like NiFe-PB@MoS2 (PB: Prussian Blue) heterostructured nanocomposite (NFPPM) catalysts were successfully synthesised to achieve significantly enhanced antibacterial activity. In the prepared heterostructure, MoS2 nanoflowers were decorated with NiFe-PB nanoparticles through an in situ growth process. The incorporation of NiFe-PB effectively improved the catalytic and photothermal activity of MoS2 under NIR irradiation. After 10 min of NIR exposure, the NFPPM nanocomposite exhibited remarkable antibacterial efficiency against Staphylococcus aureus Escherichia coli. Peroxidase-like nanozymes have been extensively explored in various biomedical applications because of their excellent catalytic properties. The as-prepared NFPPM demonstrated enhanced peroxidase-like activity, leading to superior antibacterial performance. Furthermore, this work provides a promising strategy based on adhesive nanozymes that can closely interact with bacterial surfaces, offering valuable insight into the design of highly efficient heterojunction-containing photocatalysts with superior antibacterial activity.

item.title: Molecular Structure Determines Phase Selectivity in Quasi-2D Halide Perovskites
item.description: Controlling the phase distribution in quasi-two-dimensional (2D) halide perovskites (HPs) is a crucial bottleneck for bespoke manipulation of their optoelectronic functionalities. This mainly lies in the subtle interaction between molecular spacers and inorganic precursors during crystallization that steers phase synthesizability, which has been poorly explored. Here, we investigate the synthesis spaces of two distinct quasi-2D HPs incorporating phenylethylammonium (PEA) and octylammonium (OA)-possessing comparable molecular masses but different structures and chemical properties. Utilization of a high-throughput automated experimental workflow combined with a deep-learning analytic framework allows for fully uncovering the latent synthesis landscape and distinct crystallization behaviors across the two systems. Specifically, while PEA promotes rapid crystallization and the formation of multiple low-n phases, the OA system exhibits slower crystallization and a strong preference for single-phase growth. Such a selective and controlled behavior is found to originate from the structural instability of n=1 OA2PbI4 arising from alkyl chain-induced lattice distortion. These findings demonstrate how spacer molecular structure directs crystallization pathways and phase landscapes, which offer a guideline for the rational design of phase-controlled quasi-2D HPs from conventional nonequilibrium synthetic processes, thus benefiting future optoelectronic applications.

item.title: Tracking Local Proton Activity during Hydrogen Oxidation in Nonaqueous Electrolytes
item.description: Electrochemical N2 and CO2 reduction in organic electrolytes containing proton donors offer promising routes for the electrosynthesis of ammonia and CO2-derived hydrogenated products. Hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) at the anode offers a highly attractive anodic counter reaction. Proton activity controls each of these reactions selectivity and efficiency, yet its evolution near the electrode under operating conditions is ill defined. Here, we present a rotating ring disk electrode (RRDE) method for tracking local proton activity during HOR. By simultaneously measuring the Pt disk current and the open circuit potential of the Pt ring, we monitor the conversion of proton-accepting bases to their conjugate acids using established acid–base equilibria. We demonstrate this approach using benzoic acid/benzoate (BzOH/BzO−), acetic acid/acetate (AcOH/AcO−), ethanol/ethoxide (EtOH/EtO−) and tert-butanol/butoxide, (t-BuOH/BuO−) pairs spanning a broad pKa range. The potential required to sustain HOR varies substantially between proton acceptors and does not merely follow their basicity. Our results demonstrate how RRDE measurements can probe local acid–base equilibria during electrochemical reactions, providing a basis for understanding the influence of electrolyte composition on H2 oxidation in nonaqueous solvents.

item.title: Highly active supported nickel phosphide catalyst for the semi-hydrogenation of complex, densely functionalized alkynes
item.description: Despite the outstanding performance achieved with a variety of heterogeneous semi-hydrogenation catalysts, the classic Lindlar catalyst (Pd(Pb)/CaCO3) remains the go-to choice for fine chemical synthesis due to the large substrate scope and functional group compatibility that has been repeatedly demonstrated for it. The development of highly active and chemoselective semi-hydrogenation catalysts that can not only tackle model alkynes, but complex substrates is thus crucial for a transition to lead-free, and ideally also noble-metal-free catalysts. Here we report the semi-hydrogenation of a series of complex alkynes, incorporating easily reducible functionalities as well as sulphur and nitrogen-containing heterocycles with an alumina-supported nickel phosphide catalyst. Ni2P/Al2O3 displays catalytic activity on par with the Lindlar catalyst, especially for complex, densely functionalized substrates, and its high resistance to oxidation permits benchtop storage. Notably, while a substantial loss of activity was observed with recycled Lindlar catalyst in the semi-hydrogenation of efavirenz, Ni2P/Al2O3 is readily recyclable for both simple and complex alkynes. Minimal nickel leaching in the presence of polar solvents and coordinating functional groups, along with effective performance in gram-scale reactions further validate the catalyst’s operational viability. Ni2P/Al2O3 constitutes a practical, active, and selective semi-hydrogenation catalyst for a wide variety of diversely functionalized substrates, and thus provides a lead- and palladium-free alternative to the benchmark Lindlar catalyst.

item.title: A Standard Machine-Learning Virtual Screening Pipeline Produces Candidates Indistinguishable From Random Drug-Like Compounds: A Quantitative Audit Using COX-2 As Case Study
item.description: Motivation: Machine-learning (ML) virtual screening pipelines report strong retrospective benchmark performance (Pearson R > 0.8) and convert it into prioritized candidate lists. Whether those candidates dock better than random drug-like compounds against the actual target is rarely tested. We test it.Methods: Random Forest regressors were trained on COX-2 (CHEMBL230, n = 4,445; Pearson R = 0.756, RMSE = 0.81 pIC50) and COX-1 (CHEMBL221, n = 1,652; R = 0.682, RMSE = 0.72 pIC50) and applied to 249,455 ZINC250k compounds. Potency, Lipinski, solubility-window (−1 ≤ logP ≤ 3), and PAINS filters returned 42 candidates, each annotated with predicted COX-1 selectivity, Murcko scaffold, max-Tanimoto applicability-domain coverage, synthetic accessibility (SA), and BRENK alerts. All 42 candidates and a 100-compound random ZINC250k control (sampled before any ML scoring) were docked into the chain-A binding pocket of human COX-2 (PDB 1CX2) with AutoDock Vina. Celecoxib was redocked as positive control; pose recovery was scored by heavy-atom RMSD to the crystal ligand.Results: Celecoxib redocked at −11.23 kcal/mol with 0.63 Å RMSD to the crystal ligandprotocol valid. All 42 candidates docked successfully (Vina best −11.06, median −7.58, worst −3.63 kcal/mol; 11 reached ≤ −8.0); none beat celecoxib. 39 of 42 candidates (93%) lay outside the applicability domain (T ≥ 0.40; mean max-Tanimoto = 0.243). The candidate Vina distribution was statistically indistinguishable from the random baseline (Mann-Whitney p = 0.89; Welch p = 0.68; Cohen’s d = −0.08; Hodges–Lehmann shift −0.02 kcal/mol, 95% CI [−0.42,+0.34]). ML pIC50 and Vina rankings were uncorrelated (Spearman ρ = −0.086, 95% CI [−0.35,+0.20]). The top-20 ML-prioritized candidates engaged celecoxib’s pocket residues at parity with random ZINC (Val523: 16/20 vs. 16/20; mean contact recovery 0.73 vs. 0.66). A Vina-on-training validation showed that Vina at our settings did separate genuine ChEMBL COX-2 actives from random ZINC (actives median −8.40 vs. random −7.53 kcal/mol, p = 0.006)—yet the ML candidates docked at the random level (−7.58), not the actives level. Candidates were synthesizable (SA ≤ 5 for all 42, mean 3.01); 19/42 carried BRENK alerts.Conclusions: A standard Random Forest screen at R = 0.756 produces no candidate enrichment over random ZINC by any objective measure: no docking gain, no positive ML–Vina rank correlation, 93% out-of-domain prediction. Critically, the same docking oracle does separate genuine COX-2 actives from random ZINC—so the failure is a property of the ML candidate list, not of the evaluation. The benchmark R does not predict prospective hit-finding on cross-library screens. Applicability-domain coverage and a same-library random-baseline comparison should be mandatory reporting elements in ML virtual screening papers.

item.title: MD-SOP: Sequence-based prediction of protein backbone order parameters across computational label sources
item.description: Experimental data for protein backbone N–H order parameters () are limited, which restricts model training and testing. MD-SOP was developed to predict these parameters from protein sequences using labels calculated from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in ATLAS and pseudo-labels generated by S-OPPE. ESM-C embeddings and hidden Markov model profiles were used as inputs to a bidirectional long short-term memory network. MD-only, S-OPPE-only, and mixed training were compared using two regression heads. The two datasets were split jointly by sequence similarity. Each model configuration was trained with five random seeds on the same split. Models trained and selected using one label source could predict residue-level trends in the other source, although systematic biases remained. Mixed training gave root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) between those of the two single-source models on both computational test sets. On ten experimental proteins excluded from training and model selection, the MD-only model with a single-position regression head had the lowest mean RMSE (0.109). The corresponding S-OPPE-only model had the highest mean Pearson correlation coefficient (0.860). These findings support the use of computational labels for training sequence-based order-parameter predictors. Tests across label sources provide indirect evidence of generalization when experimental data are limited. However, they do not establish that either label source is equivalent to experimental measurements. Further tests on new data splits and more independent experimental proteins are needed.

item.title: GPU acceleration of first-principles X-ray absorption spectra: an OpenACC port of XSpectra in Quantum ESPRESSO
item.description: XSpectra, the X-ray absorption module of Quantum ESPRESSO, computes K- and L-edge spectra from a Lanczos (Haydock) recursion on the self-consistent Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian of a supercell containing a core hole. In supercell calculations the recursion dominates the cost, but XSpectra had no GPU implementation, and in the GPU-enabled versions of Quantum ESPRESSO it stopped as soon as it applied the Hamiltonian. We present an OpenACC port of XSpectra for ultrasoft and projectoraugmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotentials, validated here with PAW datasets. The Lanczos vectors stay on the device for the whole recursion; the Hamiltonian and the inverse overlap operator S-1 are applied there, and only the recursion coefficients are returned to the host. The matrix that defines S-1 is built once per k point with cuBLAS. The CPU build gives the same results as before. We validate the port against the CPU code and benchmark it on a set of solids and molecules. One NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 workstation GPU runs the XSpectra step 1.6–3.6× faster than a 64-core Xeon node for 64–162-atom cells, and 1.5–3.0× faster for the whole calculation including the SCF, which runs on the CPU; for the 162-atom α-SiO2 cell, the XSpectra step for the Si K edge is accelerated by 3.6×. For small cells with dense k-point grids the CPU node is faster. On the 162-atom cell, k-point parallelization over three RTX PRO 6000 GPUs is 2.94× faster than one GPU (11× faster than the CPU node), and the run time on different GPU models is ordered by their memory bandwidth rather than by their FP64 peak. The patches are available at https://github.com/YinanWang-iis/xspectra-gpu.

item.title: Cross-Facility Materials Discovery Platform: Integrating Heterogeneous Data and Automated Experimental Pipelines into High-Throughput Workflows
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven materials discovery depends on the availability of large, highly annotated experimental datasets. However, data generated in typical materials science projects are fragmented across heterogeneous instruments, laboratories, and user facilities, each with its own formats, schedules, and degree of curation. In addition, manual sample preparation, time-consuming characterization, and changing sample form factors and holders between process steps often limit throughput and therefore dataset size. Here, we present a modular cross-facility workflow that addresses both the physical and the data bottlenecks. We combine robotic thin-film deposition, a custom robotic UV-vis setup, and high-throughput synchrotron end stations with custom, QR-code-tagged sample holders, preserving each film’s identity as it moves between experimental setups. Using Crucible, a schema-free data management platform developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, we link every sample, container, and dataset into a provenance network that traces each thin film through synthesis, deposition, characterization, and analysis. A Python client and custom web interfaces connect the Molecular Foundry with two beamlines at the Advanced Light Source and enable streamlined, high-throughput data collection pipelines. To demonstrate this workflow, we fabricated 6,105 thin films spanning 618 hybrid metal halide compounds over six months, of which approximately 3,400 were characterized by robotic grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering and 2,000 by residual gas analysis under extreme-ultraviolet exposure, generating a highly curated AI-ready materials discovery dataset that accurately reproduces a subset of matched manually prepared samples. We further demonstrate automated downstream analysis, including human-in-the-loop machine-learning classification and mechanistic evaluation of structure-property relationships. Together, the dataset and infrastructure provide a blueprint for scaling materials experimentation to facility-level AI platforms.

item.title: Temporal Rate-Shaping in Generic Reaction and Mediator-Regeneration Networks
item.description: This study examines whether generating a consumed reactant during operation can redistribute reaction throughput over a finite observation period when compared with a batch system containing the same initial reactant-equivalent inventory. Two mathematical models are developed. Model 1 is an abstract six-species reaction network in which a bimolecular primary reaction consumes A and B while a first-order auxiliary process converts precursor X into B and Y . Four configurations are compared: a baseline batch system, a replenishment system, an equal-inventory batch control, and an inert-precursor control. Adaptive numerical integration and conservation checks are used to evaluate total reaction extent, second-half extent, active-rate duration, and parameter sensitivity. In the baseline case, the replenishment configuration produces 0.109800mol of second-half extent compared with 0.040255mol for the equal-inventory batch control, a ratio of 2.728. However, the batch control achieves slightly greater total conversion, and one of 25 tested kinetic parameter pairs gives a negative second-half advantage. The result is therefore a conditional temporal redistribution effect, not a universal improvement. Model 2 extends the analysis to a dimensionless mediator-regeneration network with a conserved mediator pool and a phenomenological saturating regeneration flux. For the illustrative baseline, the regeneration model yields 0.175489 units of second-half conversion, compared with 0.019709 for the batch control, while its total conversion is lower. The regeneration-capacity sweep is non-monotonic: stronger regeneration can improve latestage conversion over part of the tested range, but excessive capacity shifts conversion toward the first half. The mediator inventory is conserved numerically to approximately machine precision. The models do not calculate electrical work, terminal voltage, Faradaic efficiency, or thermodynamic efficiency. In particular, equal initialmediator inventory is not an energy-equivalent comparison when regeneration requires external work. The contribution is a mathematical framework for analysing time-distributed availability under explicit inventory controls; physical validation remains future work.

item.title: 6,7-Difunctionalized 2-Azanorbornanes from a Bench-Stable Aziridinium Salt: Scope, Limitations, and Multigram Synthesis
item.description: 2-Azanorbornanes (2-azabicyclo[2.2.1]heptanes) are present in approved drugs, yet practical methods for their functionalization at C6 and C7 are scarce. Herein, we report a two-cycle approach to 6,7difunctionalized 2-azanorbornanes from a single aziridinium salt. The salt is prepared in two steps from cyclopentadiene on a scale of up to 300 g per run. It is a bench-stable crystalline solid that can be stored and handled as a regular reagent. In the first cycle, O-, N-, S-, F-, C-, and P-nucleophiles open the aziridinium ring at C6 with complete regio- and stereoselectivity. In the second cycle, the bromine at C7 is replaced by azide, cyanide, or fluoride with retention of configuration, or removed reductively. The approach provided conformationally restricted amino acids, diamines, and fluorinated building blocks for medicinal chemistry on a gram to multigram scale.

item.title: Distributed Assembly Theory: Distinguishing Biological Causal Depth from Information Entropy via Recursive Fragmentation
item.description: Identifying agnostic biosignatures—measurable structural properties distinguishing evolved biochemistry from abiotic matter—remains a central challenge in astrobiology and cheminformatics [1, 13, 14]. Assembly Theory (AT) addresses this boundary through the molecular Assembly Index (M_A), a measure of constructional complexity defined by the minimal number of recursive bond-joining operations required to build a molecular graph while reusing previously assembled substructures [1, 15]. However, two major criticisms challenge this framework. First, critiques grounded in Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) and Algorithmic Information Dynamics (AID) contend that M_A offers no fundamental advance over one-dimensional lossless compression, arguing that molecular assembly reduces to standard Lempel–Ziv dictionary proxies (zlib/DEFLATE and LZW) [4, 5, 7]. Second, computational critiques argue that exact M_A enumeration is intractable for complex natural products due to combinatorial subgraph explosion [1, 8].Here, we resolve this methodological impasse. We demonstrate that while canonical branch-and-bound subgraph isomorphism logic [8] is mathematically sound, legacy internal parallelization layouts (specifically untied #pragma omp task directives using shallow firstprivate object copies) exhibit a 100% segmentation-fault crash rate on cyclic macromolecules due to race-condition double-free heap corruption. To eliminate this concurrency bottleneck, we introduce an asynchronous, process-isolated orchestration architecture paired with standardized MDL V2000 graph serialization that enforces strict single-threaded execution within individual C++ traversals while expanding compile-time bitset tracking bounds to 4,096 bits. High-throughput scaling is recovered via external operating-system process isolation (ProcessPoolExecutor) across a 256 GB unified-memory compute architecture.Using this decoupled pipeline, we evaluated 397 benchmark molecules across four structural complexity classes—achieving 396 exact integer resolutions (99.75%, with 1 combinatorial-horizon timeout at 1,200 s and zero mathematical bound violations) and resolving the diterpenoid Paclitaxel (Taxol) in isolation to M_A=23. For each resolved structure, we compared exact M_A against 1D dictionary compressibility quantified via zlib/DEFLATE compressed SMILES byte cost per non-hydrogen heavy atom (C_"LZW" =L_"zlib" ("SMILES" )/N_"heavy" ) through the Causal-to-Compression Ratio (R_"MA/LZW" =M_A/C_"LZW" ) [7, 12]. Whereas 1D byte cost per heavy atom inverts physical complexity due to syntactic character redundancy—scoring simple abiotic solvents higher than complex natural products (mean C_"LZW" =2.773 vs. 1.835" bytes/heavy atom" , with "C" _20 "-" "C" _40 branched alkanes lowest at 1.573)—both exact M_A and R_"MA/LZW" exhibit strictly monotonic divergence across complexity tiers. Mean R_"MA/LZW" climbs sequentially from abiotic solvents (2.656, mean M_A=4.83) and primary metabolites (3.926, mean M_A=7.90) through stochastic "C" _20 "-" "C" _40 branched alkanes (5.704, capped at a hard abiotic ceiling of M_A≤11) to complex natural products (7.214, mean M_A=12.48, benchmark maximum R_"MA/LZW" =16.580), reaching 15.333 (M_A=23 at C_"LZW" =1.50" bytes/heavy atom" ) for Paclitaxel. These results demonstrate that evolved biochemistry combines high 3D constructional depth with modular substructure reuse—a dual topological signature that 1D string compression fails to resolve.Note on Version History: This manuscript is a comprehensive revision of our preliminary preprint, "Distributed Assembly Theory: Distinguishing Biological Causal Depth from Information Entropy via Recursive Fragmentation" (ChemRxiv, June 2026) [9]. The preliminary version utilized a heuristic BRICS retrosynthetic fragmentation approximation [3], which violated exact ⌈log_2⁡E ⌉ graph lower bounds on fused polycyclic macromolecules. This V2 manuscript supersedes the preliminary report by implementing exact C++ branch-and-bound graph enumeration [8], resolving OpenMP heap-corruption vulnerabilities, and establishing exact M_A/C_"LZW" divergence baselines.

item.title: Prediction and Determination of Monolayer Structure in Binary Ligand Mixtures on Gold Nanoparticles
item.description: Controlling multi-ligand assembly on nanoparticles (NPs) is critical for developing advanced nanomaterials for sensing, diagnostics, and therapy. Despite the importance of designing nanomaterials with tailored interfaces, it remains poorly understood how the physical and chemical driving forces will influence monolayer morphology for a variety of chemically functional ligand mixtures. In particular, terminal carboxyl and amino moieties offer diverse functionalization pathways. We systematically investigate carboxyl- and methyl-terminated alkanethiols (-COOH/-CH3) and amine- and methyl-terminated alkanethiols (-NH2/-CH3). Both binary monolayer systems included chain length mismatches ranging from 0 to 9 methylene units. We extended a quantitative framework to probe and predict mixed-ligand monolayer self-assembly by integrating matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS) experiments with configurational bias Monte Carlo (CBMC) simulations. Our results revealed that monolayer morphology is significantly impacted by the chain length difference between the chemically distinct mixtures of alkanethiols with either the mercaptocarboxylic acid or amine-functional ligands; both monolayer systems transition from randomly-mixed to phase-separated Janus-like domains as chain length difference increases. The structural asymmetry observed in the phase-separated binary monolayers offers an advantageous and programmable dual purpose platform where hydrophobic domains may impart stability while the functional domains enable targeted binding. This work provides additional insight into the tailored synthesis of multifunctional monolayer-protected ultrasmall nanoparticles for a variety of high-impact applications.

item.title: IRexp: A database of experimental infrared band lists from open-access literature
item.description: Machine-learning models for infrared (IR) spectroscopy are often trained on computed spectra, yet simulated spectra differ from measured ones, and large, open experimental IR datasets remain scarce. Here, we introduce IRexp, an open collection of 230,946 experimental IR band lists (cm⁻¹ peak positions) extracted from 19,859 open-access articles published between 2005 and 2026 and their supporting information, together with an author-entered Chemotion repository deposit. In total, 96,973 records are linked to a resolved structure, and 50,682 of these also carry author-reported ¹H and ¹³C NMR. Record quality was checked manually against the source documents and by automated consistency tests. IRexp holds more than four times as many experimental IR records as existing public IR spectral libraries, and every record keeps its source identifier and licence, with records released in licence-specific files. We expect IRexp to accelerate data-driven IR spectral prediction, automated structure elucidation, and multimodal models trained on real experimental data.

item.title: Drug-resistance phenotypes in FGFR deep mutational scanning are carried by a single-residue positional statistic that transfers across FGFR1–3 and weakens in FGFR4
item.description: Motivation: Drug-resistance mutations are a clinically central but poorly predicted phenotype: pathogenicity predictors trained on disease labels misrank them, and our recent benchmark of five static predictor families (AlphaMissense, FoldX stability, FoldX interaction energy, ThermoMPNN-D and AutoDock Vina) showed that biophysical scores predict FGFR resistance poorly. Whether supervised recalibration on functional deep mutational scanning (DMS) labels can repair this, and what feature class carries the signal, remains untested.Results: Using the DMS of the FGFR1–4 kinase domains (Tangermann et al. 2026; 7,522 unique variants) under leave-one-subtype-out validation, raw AlphaMissense correlates negatively with the resistance score in every subtype (ρ = −0.46 to −0.65), and on the binary task models built on biophysical scores reach AUROC 0.54–0.74 and never exceed the position-based model (scores 0.56–0.64 vs position 0.73–0.87 on the complete-case subset, n = 5,135). On the continuous score, a one-parameter sign flip remains the strongest recalibration. The signal is instead carried by an aligned-position prior: a parameter-free lookup of resistance rates at each aligned kinase-domain coordinate, transferred from the training subtypes. The lookup matches or exceeds a gradient-boosted model (AUROC 0.88, 0.89, 0.84, 0.70 for FGFR1–4), is strongly resistance-skewed (pure-resistance 0.86, 0.84, 0.84, 0.61; pure-activating 0.62, 0.60, 0.42, 0.46), peaks at single-residue resolution, sits 0.16–0.30 above the strongest clinical-hotspot baseline, and reaches AUPRC 0.31–0.48 with 37–63% precision in the top 50; a two-stage blend that resolves within-site ordering raises this to 36–64% with a tie-free ranking at no AUROC cost. The prior transfers across drugs (pemigatinib → futibatinib, 0.74–0.83) and across FGFR1–3, weakening for FGFR4.Conclusion: FGFR resistance phenotypes are recoverable from a homology-transferred positional label statistic — a lookup table, not a fitted model; the lookup alone recovers the discrimination, and a within-site score ranker refines the top of the list without adding discrimination. The statistic is specific to resistance, contains information beyond known clinical hotspots, and transfers across drugs within the FGFR inhibitor class.

item.title: Understanding a Helix Reverse Path in Perfluoroalkanes from a Neural Network Potential
item.description: The helical handedness of perfluoroalkanes and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) is considered to reverse through localized helix-reversal defects. Earlier studies with empirical and semiempirical potentials described how such defects form and move. The helix, however, originates from hyperconjugation, and the reversal pathway of a single molecule has not yet been examined with a potential that includes this quantum-chemical effect. Here we trained a MACE potential on DF-MP2-F12 data for C4F10–C7F16 and located three reversal pathways of C24F50 by CI-NEB: a concerted pathway through the all-trans (D2h) structure, a single-wall pathway, and a twin-wall pathway. For C24F50, the concerted barrier is 13.74 kcalmol−1, far above those of the single-wall pathway (2.01 kcalmol−1) and the twin-wall pathway (4.82 kcalmol−1); the concerted barrier grows linearly with chain length, whereas the single-wall barrier does not depend on it. At 25 ◦C, the single-wall pathway is about 108 times faster than the concerted one for C24F50 when the prefactors are assumed equal, so the concerted reversal of an isolated chain is kinetically very unfavorable. For C13F28–C15F32, DFT calculations show that the frequency of the wall mode depends on the position of the wall, so wall-containing conformations can contribute to the broad defectrelated band in the ATR-IR spectra of these short-chain perfluoroalkanes. The growth of the low-wavenumber component from 20 to 70 ◦C is consistent with an increasing thermal population of these conformations. In the single-wall path, a moving wall also rotates the chain about its axis. Combined with crystal simulations in the literature, this supports the screw-like motion proposed for PTFE, in which the rotation of a chain is accompanied by a translation along its axis.

item.title: Mechanistic Pitfalls of Unbalanced Excited-State Descriptions across Competing Pathways: Thiophene as a Case Study
item.description: A balanced description of excited states remains challenging even for small organic molecules. For thiophene, we show that an unbalanced description can conceal an entire relaxation pathway. Comparing SA-CASSCF and RMS-CASPT2 potential energy curves toward the ring-opening (RO) and ring-puckering (RP) conical intersections, we identify the state carrying the molecule to each crossing, termed the carrier state. Dynamic electron correlation leaves the RO carrier (πσ*) state nearly unchanged but strongly stabilizes the RP carrier (ππ*) state. Consequently, the RP channel opens in RMS-CASPT2-based surface hopping simulations (26% versus 67% for RO), whereas it was absent in previous CASSCF-based ones. Through this RP channel, molecules return almost exclusively to the ring-closed form, thereby shifting the predicted photoproduct distribution toward nearly equal rearranged and ring-closed fractions. Concealment of a competing pathway is not apparent from Franck–Condon energetics alone but exposed by tracking the states along paths to the crossings.

item.title: Programmable Nanofluidic Confinement: From Static Nanotopographies to Reversible Electrokinetic Trapping
item.description: Single-molecule analysis increasingly relies on the ability to immobilize, confine, and manipulate biomolecules in solution. Nanofluidic devices provide a powerful route to this goal by using embedded nanotopographies on-chip to define free-energy landscapes that enable spatial manipulation, transport, confinement, and conformations that can be leveraged for biomedical applications. One classic example for molecular confinement is DNA extension in nanochannels, which has allowed for high-throughput genomic sequencing on-chip. Classic nanofluidic devices however are often limited by the static nature of their confinement landscapes, which are fixed by the static geometry of the device after fabrication, not allowing for real-time manipulation. Examples from optics (e.g. optical tweezers, optical lattices, holographic optical tweezers) demonstrate that, in principle, it is possible to achieve high-throughput dynamic control by using external fields to impose and alter confinement. In this review, we discuss different methods to engineer tunable free energy landscapes for nanoscale confinement of molecules. We first describe fabrication strategies and static nanofluidic geometries, emphasizing how top-down nanotopographies impose equilibrium molecular conformations. We then examine mechanically and pneumatically tunable platforms that modulate confinement after fabrication, followed by more tunable field-based approaches that use electrokinetic, thermophoretic, optical, and plasmonic effects to localize, concentrate, and manipulate molecules in solution. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies that combine lithographically defined nanofluidic arrays with externally applied fields to create reversible and dynamically tunable confinement landscapes. Such approaches point toward a new generation of nanofluidic devices in which single molecules can be immobilized, released, and driven between conformational states in real time, enabling high-throughput studies of non-equilibrium biomolecular dynamics and active molecular control on chip.

item.title: Single-Step Assembly at Physiological pH of Lipid Nanoparticles Encapsulating a Single Polynucleotide
Digital twin reconstruction of red blood cell aging using Raman chemometrics and systems modeling
item.description: Red blood cell (RBC) storage aging involves progressive metabolic and oxidative alterations that compromise membrane integrity and transfusion quality. However, conventional endpoint measurements provide limited information on individual aging dynamics and their predictability. This study presents an experimentally constrained digital twin framework integrating Raman spectral analysis, chemometric modeling, and mechanistic simulation to reconstruct RBC aging trajectories and predict donor-specific hemolysis. Longitudinal Raman spectra and biochemical measurements from packed RBC units stored for eight weeks were analyzed using principal component analysis, least squares decomposition, multivariate curve resolution–alternating least squares, and partial least squares regression. A MATLAB/SimBiology model coupled glucose metabolism, redox regulation, oxidative membrane deterioration, and hemoglobin release. The integrated approach resolved continuous biochemical trajectories characterized by glucose depletion, lactate accumulation, and progressive hemolysis. Despite broadly comparable metabolic kinetics, female-derived RBCs showed slower hemolysis than male-derived RBCs (0.05 ± 0.03 versus 0.40 ± 0.14 week-1). Early Raman spectral features predicted donor-specific hemolysis kinetics (R2 = 0.69), supporting their potential as predictive biomarkers of storage stability. The digital twin reproduced observed metabolic and hemolysis trajectories and implicated hydrogen peroxide regulation, glutathione availability, and GSH/GSSG turnover as candidate contributors to sex-dependent differences. By linking high-dimensional spectroscopic signals with interpretable mechanistic modeling, this framework provides a strategy for tracking RBC storage deterioration and estimating individual aging behavior from early measurements. It may support future development of personalized blood-quality assessment tools.

item.title: Coupling Metallaarsinidene and Methylene Groups to an Arsavinyl [As=CH2]– Ligand; a Softer Pnictovinyl Is a Harder Molecular Switch
From De Novo Molecular Design to Experimentally Validated Protein-Protein Interaction Modulators
item.description: Identifying bioactive small molecules requires balancing target affinity with physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties compatible with drug development. This is particularly challenging in the development of small-molecule modulators of protein–protein interactions (PPIs) due to the structural complexity of protein interfaces. Here, we developed an integrated workflow combining de novo molecular design with similarity-guided identification of existing compounds from public chemical libraries. We applied this strategy to neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1), a calcium-binding protein whose interactions with multiple partners regulate synaptic function, making it an attractive target for modulating neuronal signaling. REINVENT4-based molecular generation incorporated predicted binding to the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice, synthetic accessibility, and CNS-relevant ADMET properties, including blood–brain barrier permeability. Generated structures guided the selection of commercially available analogues. Experimental validation supported the effectiveness of this AI-guided strategy: 11 of the 12 tested compounds bound NCS-1, including 5 with micromolar affinities. In situ protein–protein interaction assays further confirmed the modulatory activity of selected compounds, identifying, to our knowledge, the first small-molecule enhancers of the NCS-1/cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1R) interaction. CB1R is an attractive pharmacological target implicated in neuronal signaling, whose activity is regulated by NCS-1. High-resolution crystal structures revealed how these modulators engage the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice, providing structural insights into ligand recognition and suggesting a mechanism of action. These findings connect generative molecular design with experimentally accessible NCS-1 ligands and provide chemical tools and structural insights for investigating NCS-1-dependent regulation of CB1R.

item.title: Measuring the Membrane Protein-Bound Lipidome
item.description: Lipids play diverse physiological roles in energy storage, signaling, and cell structure. Another less appreciated role is as allosteric modulators of membrane proteins. However, it is challenging to determine the identify and affinity of lipids interacting with a given membrane protein target. In this review, we discuss analytical advances in using lipidomics to profile lipids bound to specific membrane proteins, which we will refer to as protein-lipid interactomics. We will consider the challenges of solubilizing and isolating the membrane protein while retaining relevant lipid interactions, focusing on detergents and lipid nanoparticles made with polymer, peptide, and protein scaffolds. We will also discuss aspects of overall experiment design, including basic identification, quantitative experiments, progressive delipidation, and lipid exchange to probe the strength of lipid interactions. Finally, we conclude with key questions, current analytical challenges, and proposed future directions for this emerging field.

item.title: Analytic Hessian for mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory
item.description: Mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory (MRSF-TDDFT) describes diradicals and nearly degenerate states largely free of the spin contamination of spin-flip (SF) TDDFT, but its Hessian has been available only numerically. Within the Tamm–Dancoff approximation, we derive and implement the analytic Hessian of MRSF-TDDFT with restricted open-shell references, including SF-TDDFT as a special case, and the analytic polarizability derivative for excited-state Raman intensities. For stilbene, the analytic Hessian reproduces finite-difference frequencies to within 0.07 cm⁻¹ at one-nineteenth of the estimated three-point finite-difference cost. The Hessians show that the twisted S₁ intermediate (the phantom state) is an MRSF minimum and characterize the diradical S₀ saddle point. Computed ¹³C isotope shifts are consistent with the assignment of the S₁ resonance Raman band of the central C=C bond; at the phantom state, this band lies about 170 cm⁻¹ lower than at the planar S₁ minimum, a candidate marker of the twist. At the saddle point, SF-TDDFT gives energies and a reaction-coordinate curvature close to those of MRSF-TDDFT, but in a direction orthogonal to the reaction coordinate its Hessian has an unphysical mode at 6005 cm⁻¹ and, at a nearby point on the path, an imaginary frequency of 3358i cm⁻¹. S₀ and the MS = 0 component of T₁ are roots of the same SF response matrix; spin contamination couples them in the Hessian through a term inversely proportional to their gap. MRSF-TDDFT, with separate singlet and triplet response matrices, has no such term. Spin contamination can thus affect curvatures much more than energies.

item.title: Ultrathin high-aspect-ratio chiral gold nanofibers
item.description: Chirality, a fundamental characteristic of nature, plays a decisive role in molecular recognition, catalysis, and cellular organization. Translating this asymmetry into synthetic systems has the potential to unlock new functionalities at the interface of nanoscience and biology. Here, we report the synthesis of high-aspect-ratio chiral gold nanofibers, a class of one-dimensional chiral plasmonic materials, fabricated via a seedless, ligand-assisted growth method using D/L-cysteine as chiral inducers. The growth mechanism seems to involve initial particle and aggregate formation, the emergence of short filaments associated with these domains, and subsequent elongation and interconnection into nanofibers. Surfactant attachment onto the particle surface may have facilitated anisotropic growth within this pathway, but their organization and any restructuring during synthesis cannot be established. The resulting chiral gold nanofibers exhibit pronounced, mirror-symmetric circular dichroism signals and characteristic plasmonic resonances, confirming their intrinsic structural chirality. Further, 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy analysis indicates areas of the nanofibers with continuous variations of the crystal orientation, which can be linked to the observed topographical chirality of the gold nanofibers. Altogether, this effort establishes a simple and scalable route to fabricate chiral gold architectures with potential applications in asymmetric catalysis, optical sensing and bio-instructive scaffoldings.

item.title: The Hg + O → HgO Reaction on the Triplet Potential Energy Surface: A CCSD(T)/VTST Investigation
item.description: The gas-phase reaction of atomic mercury (Hg) with ground-state atomic oxygen (O(3P)) is relevant to mercury oxidation in combustion flue gases and non-thermal plasma environments. However, no experimental rate constants for this reaction are available in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Chemical Kinetics Database. Here, the reaction is investigated using density functional theory at the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/SDD+6-311++G(3df,3pd) level, combined with CCSD(T) single-point energy calculations. A relaxed potential energy surface (PES) scan was performed along the Hg–O coordinate from 1.80 to 10.00 Å on the spin-free triplet surface. Within this range, the calculated potential energy decreases as the atoms approach, and no entrance-channel barrier above the separated-reactant energy is observed at the sampled points. The equilibrium Hg–O bond length is 2.14 Å, and the dissociation energy D0 is 7.54 kcal mol-1. Variational RRKM calculations using generalized transition states yield a rate constant of 6.47 × 10-10 cm3 molecule-1 s-1 at 300 K, with weak temperature dependence over 300–500 K. The calculated rate constants are compared with Wilcox’s forward association rate expression, accounting for differences in electronic-state descriptions and kinetic treatments. These results provide kinetic data for the Hg + O reaction at low temperatures and a basis for evaluating the atomic-oxygen pathway in mercury oxidation models relevant to non-thermal plasma applications.

item.title: Side-Reaction Pathways and Catalyst Deactivation during ATRP of N-Vinylpyrrolidone
item.description: The atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) of N-vinylpyrrolidone (NVP) remains challenging due to the low activation of the vinyl group and the prevalence of competing side reactions. In this work, we systematically investigated the polymerization of NVP using alkyl bromide initiators and Cu(Me6Cyclam)Br-based catalysts under a range of solvent environments and monomer concentrations. 1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H-NMR) kinetic studies revealed extensive monomer consumption through competing pathways, including hydrolysis, dimerization, and solvent-mediated addition reactions, which significantly suppressed productive propagation. Several reaction intermediates and by-products were identified and structurally characterized, including the previously proposed compound 1,1-bis-(N-2-oxopyrrolidinyl)ethane, which was isolated and confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and multidimensional NMR spectroscopy. Comparative solvent studies showed that protic and polar media promote acid-catalyzed transformations of NVP, likely triggered by in situ generation of HBr through halide displacement from the copper catalyst. Increasing monomer concentration partially favored propagation but did not eliminate competing reactions. To circumvent these limitations, a PLA-based macroinitiator strategy was employed, enabling the synthesis of amphiphilic PVP-b-PLA diblock copolymers with improved polymerisation efficiency. Mechanistic analysis suggests that propagation suppression arises from a combination of catalyst deactivation, solvent-mediated halide displacement, and acid-catalyzed side reactions that consume monomer. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the complex reactivity of Nvinylpyrrolidone under ATRP conditions and highlight key factors limiting controlled radical polymerization of low-activated vinyl amide monomers.

item.title: Mechanistic Determinants of Passive Permeation in Binary Lipid Membranes from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description: Passive permeation is a fundamental determinant of pharmacokinetics. The models that simulate permeation pathways and predict their energetic requirements need to account for the complexity of biological membranes. However, the impact of lipid bilayer composition on the thermodynamics of the passive permeation process is not yet fully understood. This study systematically evaluates how specific lipid types influence the free energy profiles through binary lipid bilayers for six xenobiotics with structural diversity: amantadine, diclofenac, metoprolol, pindolol, ranitidine, and scopolamine. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted using MemCross, an all-atom MD protocol based on the Accelerated Weight Histogram (AWH) method, for five binary lipid mixtures. The bilayer models combined 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) with cholesterol (CHOL), 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (POPE), 1,2-diarachidonoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DAPC), or N-stearoyl-D-erythro-sphingosylphosphorylcholine (SM18) to represent the lipid diversity of human plasma cell membranes. Our results demonstrate the lipid features that significantly modulate the free energy landscapes. Permeation appeared governed jointly by lipid composition and the intrinsic molecular properties of the permeants. We identify a series of mechanistic descriptors that drive the permeation process, explaining how they collectively contribute to passive permeation outcomes. Based on this knowledge, multivariate models were established, identifying key descriptors that can be obtained from rapid non-biased MD simulations.

item.title: FLAMES – A flexible and extensible code for Monte Carlo simulations of nanoporous materials
item.description: Molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations are the cornerstone for computational studies of adsorption in nanoporous materials such as zeolites, Metal-Organic Frameworks, and Covalent Organic Frameworks. Currently, most of these simulations rely on classical force fields, which are often limited in their ability to describe specific interactions or the intrinsic flexibility of the host framework. Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a powerful alternative, offering near ab initio accuracy while remaining computationally feasible, potentially capturing framework flexibility and complex potential energy surfaces. Despite this promise, there is a significant gap, as current tools implementing MLIPs are often general-purpose codes adapted for adsorption or in-house solutions. Here, we introduce FLAMES (Flexible Lattice Adsorption by Monte Carlo Engine Simulation), a new software package designed to perform Monte Carlo-based simulations of nanoporous materials using MLIPs and other energy calculation methods, paving the way for more accurate and physically realistic molecular simulations. We detailed the implementation of different methodologies, including Widom insertion, Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC), hybrid GCMC/MD, and Transition Matrix Monte Carlo simulations, presenting validation examples for each method and evaluating the performance and accuracy of different energy calculation methodologies.

item.title: Pre-training on Quantum Mechanical Properties Improves ADMET Prediction
Intermediate Precision of Single-Molecule Break-Junction Conductance: Measurement, Uncertainty Budget, and Design Rules
item.description: A break-junction experiment reports a molecule’s conductance from thousands of junctions recorded in one session, with an uncertainty computed from those same junctions. That uncertainty describes one session. It does not say how much the value would change if the experiment were repeated on another day with a new tip, substrate and solution. We measure this change on archived recordings of DNA:RNA duplexes that include repeat sessions at identical settings. Across seven pairs of sessions, the session-to-session standard deviation of the median conductance is a factor of 1.46 (95% interval 1.28 to 2.15), 6.4 times the usual error bar. Five ways of removing it, each tested under pre-registration, did not work. A value from a single session therefore carries an expanded uncertainty of a factor of 2.4. Spreading the same number of traces over more sessions reduces it, and we give the number of sessions a comparison needs. Public data from a second laboratory show the same effect.

item.title: Unlocking Nb2O5 for Thermocatalytic CO2 Hydrogenation via Mutual Reconstruction across Metal-Niobia Interfaces
item.description: Thermocatalytic CO2 hydrogenation could efficiently take place at the interfaces between transition metals and reducible oxides, such as CeO2, TiO2, ZrO2, and In2O3, whose oxygen vacancies play catalytic roles in adsorbing and activating CO2. In contrast, Nb2O5 has not been widely recognized as a functional oxide to facilitate CO2 activation when interfaced with transition metals. In this study, we show that the reduction of several transition metal/Nb2O5 catalysts unlocks the CO2 activation activity of Nb2O5, demonstrating considerable higher activity towards CO2 hydrogenation than their Nb-free counterparts. Most notably, the Rh/Nb2O5 interface, supported on SBA-15, shows the most profound promotional effect for CO2 methanation relative to Nb-free 2Rh/SBA-15 catalyst. At 200 °C, the optimized 2Rh5Nb/SBA-15 catalyst affords 37.2- and 13.3-fold increases in specific reaction rate and turnover frequency, respectively, relative to Nb-free 2Rh/SBA-15. Spectroscopic characterizations and density functional theory calculations suggest that during catalyst pre-reduction in H2, interfacial hydrogen transfer from Rh promotes the formation of defect-rich NbOx. The reduced NbOx in turn facilitates extensive electronic interaction with Rh, resulting in the formation of dispersed Rhδ+ species and abundant Rhδ⁺-Ov-Nb4+ interfacial ensembles. These interfacial ensembles represent highly active centers for CO2 methanation through a COOH-mediated pathway, with CO2 activation on regenerable oxygen vacancies playing a key role in the catalytic cycle, while the strongly adsorbed CO* limits the subsequent hydrogenation via CO. The present findings establish transition metal/NbOx interface as a new structural platform for designing metal-oxide catalysts for hydrogenation and deoxygenation reactions, while expanding material space for designing robust CO2 hydrogenation catalysts beyond the existing library of reducible oxides.

item.title: Using potential derivatives to reduce the cost of rectangular collocation: a general and versatile approach for computational vibrational spectroscopy without a potential energy surface
item.description: We modify the exact Cartesian kinetic energy operator, rectangular collocation approach of Manzhos and Carrington [J. Chem. Phys. 145 (2016) 224110] by using information contained in potential derivatives to decrease the number of required potential points. We show that this makes it possible to substantially reduce the number of collocation points, which is important, in particular, when energies are computed directly ab initio. Vibrational band intensities are also computed. We first demonstrate the method on Cl2CO and compare to high-accuracy Smolyak collocation calculations on an accurate potential energy surface (PES). Sub-cm-1 accuracy is obtained with a few thousand Gaussian basis functions and potential points. A spectrum computed directly from DFT energies and a comparison to GVPT2 (generalized vibrational perturbation theory) are also presented. We then consider LiCO2 as a more anharmonic case, for which a quartic force field potential is less reliable, and which also serves as a surrogate model for a catalytic system (mimicking CO2 bond weakening by charge donation). The rectangular collocation method is used to compute the spectrum of LiCO2 directly from ab initio energies and to compare to GVPT2. The method is implemented as a Claude Skill and is easily usable by anyone on any molecule. The method is a general and versatile tool for anharmonic computational vibrational spectroscopy. It does not require a PES and no coupling is neglected.

item.title: Sustained Radiopacity of Biodegradable Iodinated Polyether Blends for Tracking Long-Term Degradation in Medical Devices
item.description: Longitudinal monitoring of biomedical devices is emerging as the next phase of personalized medicine, enabling individualized treatment plans based on radiological evaluation of devices over time. However, incorporation of a contrast agent is necessary to functionalize polymeric devices for imaging, but must be balanced by changes in device properties and biocompatibility. Here we demonstrate the use of a novel polymer blend as a potential material for biomedical devices incorporating imaging functionality, consisting of 90% biodegradable poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA 50:50) matrix and 10% of an iodinated block co-polymer, poly(ethylene oxide)-co-poly(epichlorohydrin) (PEO-PECH). Addition of the iodinated PEOPECH produced porous radiopaque phantom devices with up to 3 wt% iodine. The porous phantoms remained CT-visible for the duration of a 12-week in vitro degradation study, with changes in attenuation correlating to changes in apparent density. Phantom mechanics and mass loss were affected by PECH molecular weight and iodine content in the blend but remained comparable to properties of clinical devices. During degradation, iodine was released from phantoms at a steady rate. The iodine remained molecularly bound to the polyether, which was lost more slowly than the PLGA matrix. The stable degradation and consistent attenuation make this blend promising for use in biomedical devices.

item.title: Recipes for a Broad, Low-Barrier AI Bootcamp in Chemistry
item.description: Artificial intelligence literacy is becoming an important component of chemical education and workforce preparation as AI transforms chemical research and professional practice. In the late summer of 2026, we organized a 30-hour AI bootcamp for the incoming graduate students in chemistry, biochemistry, and the broader community. Here, we discuss the main goals and design principles of the event and summarize several teaching modules that can be combined to design AI bootcamps of different lengths and scopes. Unlike a formal course on the topic, our core intention was to provide multiple starting points for the participants to self-explore and adopt AI tools for their own learning and research without requiring specialized knowledge of mathematics or computer programming. Key lessons included the strong dependence of outcomes on students’ AI literacy and model choice, the value of hands-on and discussion-based activities, and the need for a modular curriculum that can be updated rapidly as AI tools evolve.

item.title: Biomolecular Recognition Programs Fusion and Segregation of Orthogonal DNA Condensates
item.description: Controlling interactions between synthetic compartments is essential for building responsive, reconfigurable molecular systems. Here, we demonstrate that biomolecular recognition programs the fusion of orthogonal DNA-based condensates. To do that, we re-engineered ligand-functionalized DNA nanostars whose orthogonal sticky-end interactions drive phase separation into initially immiscible condensate populations. Addition of a bridging bivalent protein introduces heterotypic connections that promote condensate association, coalescence, and mixing. Through proteolytic cleavage of the biomolecular receptor, we can then restore segregation of the condensate populations. We demonstrate this approach using antigen-functionalized nanostars, with IgG antibodies inducing fusion and papain triggering segregation. We then extend the approach to thrombin-mediated fusion of condensates displaying aptamers for distinct thrombin exosites, followed by trypsintriggered segregation. A mean-field model coupled to phase-field dynamics reproduces the observed morphologies and suggests competition between antigen recognition and neighboring sticky-end bonding as a possible mechanism allowing efficient mixing. These results establish biomolecular recognition as a modular means of dynamically rewiring the composition and connectivity of synthetic compartments without redesigning the DNA interactions that drive their initial formation.

item.title: Marine Exopolysaccharide Diabolican Enhances the Physical Properties of Collagen Hydrogels via a Temperature-Dependent Polyionic Complexation
item.description: Collagens and glycosaminoglycans are essential components of the extracellular matrix, providing key biochemical and mechanical properties. Type I collagen and hyaluronan (HA) are therefore widely used in tissue engineering to mimic the characteristics of human tissues. However, native HA does not significantly improve the properties of collagen hydrogels when combined with this biopolymer. In this study, the marine exopolysaccharide diabolican (HE800 strain), which exhibits structural similarities to HA, was evaluated as an alternative glycosaminoglycan for combination with type I collagen. Mixing collagen with diabolican led to the formation of polyionic complexes (PICs), even under conditions of high osmotic strength. Complex formation depended on both the molecular weight of diabolican and temperature. Performing the mixing on ice slowed down complexation, enabling the preparation of homogeneous hydrogels. The interplay between PIC formation and collagen gelation generated composite hydrogels with significantly improved physical properties when high-molecular-weight (HMW) diabolican was used, doubling the mechanical strength compared to pure collagen. Encapsulated fibroblasts remained viable, adopted a spindle shaped morphology, proliferated, and did not induce hydrogel contraction until day seven. Importantly, these advantages were achieved without chemical functionalization or crosslinking. Overall, HMW diabolican represents a promising alternative to hyaluronan for tissue engineering applications.

item.title: A shared formulation design space reveals poly(2-ethyl-2oxazoline) chain length as a determinant of lipid nanoparticle performance and relative organ distribution
item.description: The interface between lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and their biological environment represents a key determinant of biodistribution. Here, we investigated poly(2-ethyl-2oxazoline) (PEtOx)-lipids as an adaptable component of this interface and determined how polymer chain length affects LNP formulation as well as biological behavior. Rather than comparing different polymers with a single nominal formulation composition, we first mapped the pharmaceutical design space of four PEtOx-lipids containing average chain lengths of 20, 34, 49, or 71 repeating units and identified formulation conditions that supported acceptable LNP formation. This shared design space subsequently enabled the comparison of chain-length-dependent effects under pharmaceutically viable conditions. Increasing PEtOx chain length decreased the apparent hydrophobicity of the PEtOx-lipids and was associated with progressively smaller LNP diameters, lower mRNA encapsulation efficiencies, and a narrower formulation space in which predefined criteria for size, polydispersity, and mRNA loading were met concomitantly. Optimized PEtOx-LNPs mediated mRNA expression across multiple primary and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cell types with limited effects on cell viability. Pooled in vivo DNA barcoding of the PEtOx20-, PEtOx34-, and PEtOx49-LNPs revealed chain-length-dependent differences in relative organ barcode distribution, with shorter chains shifting relative distribution toward spleen and pancreas and away from bone marrow and liver. Together, these findings establish PEtOx chain length as an independent LNP design parameter and demonstrate a formulation-space-based strategy for comparing polymeric excipients without relying on a single predefined formulation composition.

item.title: Stability and Raman Spectra of Carbon Nanotube Fragments across Chirality and Length
item.description: Bare-ended carbon nanotube (CNT) fragments restructure at their rims. Geometry screening and density functional vibrational analysis identify 13 local minima on the restricted-singlet surface; six have stable restricted solutions. Energy per carbon, fitted to the inverse squared mean optimized diameter and separate initial armchair-like and zigzag-like rim fractions (R2 = 0.993), gives effective end coefficients of 2.12 and 2.64 eV per initial rim carbon, respectively. Eleven minima contain 58 short end pairs and 58 high-frequency, mainly collective pair-stretching modes. In three armchair minima with stable restricted solutions, the pair-stretch band rises from 1994–2016 cm−1 in (3,3) to 2046–2099 cm−1 in (5,5) as mean pair length falls from 1.235 to 1.228 Å; hydrogen capping of (3,3) lengthens the pairs to 1.338 Å and removes the band. With symmetry retained, capping removes all imaginary modes of (0,3) and (2,2) and reduces those of (0,4) from eight to two. Releasing symmetry yields minima with stable restricted solutions for all three. In five chiral minima, unrestricted solutions place nearly full, opposite spins on one isolated twocoordinate carbon per end. Selective capping stabilizes closed-shell (2,3) and retains the band. Unrestricted relaxation also retains it, with 4.14-fold lower total Raman activity than the restricted reference.

item.title: Phosphorus-Functionalized Carbon Quantum Dot-Doped Alginate Beads for Rapid and High-Capacity Recovery of Rare Earth Elements
item.description: Recovering rare earth elements (REEs) from waste streams requires adsorbents that combine rapid uptake, high capacity, and effective regeneration. Here, phosphorus-functionalized carbon quantum dots immobilized on alginate beads (P-CQD/ALG) were developed to integrate REE-binding functionality with a readily separable solid form. First, phosphorus functionalization (P-CQD/ALG) showed substantially higher Ce3+ removal than pristine alginate and unmodified or nitrogen-functionalized CQD composites, suggesting P-CQD/ALG as an optimal adsorbent. Second, P-CQD/ALG also achieved fast, strong, and selective removal of 11 REEs at 78%–95% after 60 min in synthetic solutions at pH 6.8, while uptake of most other common metals was ≤9%. One exception was that Fe3+ outcompeted most REEs, identifying the requirement for iron pre-treatment. Spectroscopic characterization and uptake trends suggest electrostatic attraction and coordination with phosphorus-containing oxygen groups as major mechanisms. Third, Langmuir adsorption capacities reached 301–430 mg/g for Ce3+ and Er3+, 1.1–36 times higher than the existing materials. The capacity-normalized cost (0.05–0.07 $/kg per mg/g) was also 7–3780 times lower than other materials. Lastly, dilute HNO3 (0.05 M) enabled Ce3+ desorption and repeated adsorption over five cycles. These findings identify P-CQD/ALG as a promising platform for REE recovery, with further validation needed in real wastewaters.

item.title: Divergent Synthesis of Diazaspiroalkanes through Spirolactam Intermediates
item.description: The use of spirocyclic diamines in molecular design requires both access to the desired framework and control over the nitrogen available for functionalization. We describe a divergent synthesis that addresses these requirements through common spirolactam intermediates. Starting from three commercially available methyl N-Boc cyclic amino esters, cyanoalkylation and nitrile reduction/lactamization afforded six frameworks. Two complementary benzyl/Boc sequences then delivered 11 mono-Boc diamines in final preparations of 1.8-25 g, including five pairs with opposite protection arrangements. This work extends established lactam-based chemistry across ring size, nitrogen connectivity, and protection site through a shared set of intermediates. The study also distinguishes limitations in pipecolate cyanoethylation, seven-membered lactam formation, and final debenzylation of one [3.6] derivative, which should guide selection of a productive route. Alongside the final diamines, the NH-containing lactams and monobenzyl intermediates provide additional points for molecular elaboration. Their preparative accessibility enables future studies of how changes in spirodiamine connectivity and attachment site affect the properties of more complex molecules.

item.title: Kinetic-thermodynamic symmetry breaking in reversible two-step polycondensation
item.description: Reversible step-growth polycondensation underpins the industrial manufacture of polyamides, polyesters and polycarbonates. Yet its classical Carothers–Flory description, built on Flory’s principle of equal reactivity and on a closed-system treatment, leaves a family of recurring process anomalies outside any single theoretical framework. Here we extend the asymmetric two-step pairing scheme of the companion theory with a reverse selectivity β and introduce an independent activity factor χ for the by-product (water), obtaining a closed-form, three-parameter theory of the equilibrium structure (Ω, K̂1 ≡ K1/χ; r), with Ω ≡ 4K2/K1 = 2α/β. Within the single three-parameter map, we relax both idealizations at once (equal reactivity and the closed system) and obtain closed forms for the equilibrium state: a cubic equation for the free A end-group concentration σ with a unique physical root, exact insensitivity to the rate-level asymmetry α (a catalyst changes the rate, never the equilibrium), and exact recovery of the Flory–Schulz most-probable distribution at Ω = 1. For the system under a time-dependent by-product activity we predict three falsifiable high-vacuum scaling laws, σ ∝ χ1/2, the total cyclic oligomer content ∝ χ1/2 and the residual monomer content ∝ χ, together with a three-regime scaling law for the dominant relaxation mode whose marginal branch at exact stoichiometry scales as χ−1/2. Each exponent can be obtained as the slope of a double-logarithmic plot from measurements that existing equipment can provide. Eight recurring process anomalies are mapped onto the parameters with explicitly graded evidence, and a single calibration point provides a reference point for the framework: the sealed-tube PA6 free end-group concentration σ ≈ 0.25 inverts in closed form to Ω ≈ 496. The framework thereby extends the Carothers–Flory paradigm from a closed, equal-reactivity idealization to the open, kinetically asymmetric regime in which industrial polycondensation actually operates.

item.title: Site-Selective Peripheral Aryl Substitution Tunes Red-to-Near-Infrared Fluorescence in Thienopyrazine-Fused Pyrene Heteroacenes
item.description: We report four thienopyrazine-fused pyrene heteroacenes with aryl substituents varied at the pyrene core and flanking thiophene rings. Compounds 1–3 exhibit neat-film photoluminescence quantum yields of 64–88% at 564–589 nm, whereas compound 4 displays an emission maximum at 767 nm in solution. Single-crystal analysis of 2 shows that cofacial p–p interactions between the central aromatic cores are impeded. The results show that both the position and identity of peripheral aryl substituents influence the photoluminescence properties of a common heteroacene framework.

item.title: Electronic versus magnetic descriptors of excited-state (anti)aromaticity: a critical assessment for singlet and triplet states
item.description: Excited-state aromaticity (ESA) and antiaromaticity (ESAA) are important concepts for understanding photochemical and photophysical processes. To quantify their extent and to follow ESA gain and ESAA relief, it would be beneficial to have aromaticity indices that are readily computable for higher excited states, applicable independently of the spin multiplicity, and suitable for non-equilibrium geometries. However, current aromaticity indices remain difficult to evaluate beyond the lowest triplet state and away from equilibrium structures. Within this work, we evaluate the feasibility of using electronic aromaticity indices (EAIs) derived from time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) as a lightweight and easily applicable measure of ES(A)A. The results are compared with complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) and DFT computations, considering both EAIs and nucleus-independent chemical shifts (NICS). Using para-quinodimethane, benzene, and naphthalene as test systems, we find qualitative agreement between EAIs computed with TDDFT and CASSCF. Comparing EAIs and NICS, we find agreement for the lowest triplet states, but opposing aromaticity/antiaromaticity assignments are obtained for the singlet states. Furthermore, NICS provide an intuitive picture of ESA gain and ESAA relief upon structural relaxation, whereas EAIs do not show this consistently. In summary, EAIs and NICS are both promising for quantifying ES(A)A, but clear pitfalls exist: both should be applied with care, and the meaning of (anti)aromaticity in higher, multiconfigurational excited states warrants further study.
